### Tier-up of hot first-stage code: design note (2026-11-05)

The coordinator's item (C): before building the tier-up, explain the costs the probes found
(Splay's string concatenation through its helper, RayTrace's constructor forwarder, chai), and
design the way back from a stale baked shape in operator chains, with the tier-up at the last
checkpoint. Probes (not for landing): p2-tierup-probe 42f32e46, -probe2 f309b791, -probe3
2c5b3943 (record "Compact baseline templates: tier-up of hot first-stage code, measured before
building"), and two over the fallbacks: -probe4 4fe6d5c7 (call counts in the constructor
forwarder, TRUST_JS_PROBE_COUNTS; a record filter, TRUST_JS_PROBE_RECFILTER) and -probe5
d293f04f (tier-up only at a checkpoint whose feedback is unchanged, TRUST_JS_TIERUP_STABLE).

SUMMARY

Three things stand between the tier-up and a net win, and two of them cost main today:

1. A recompiled chunk's feedback records go through its transformed vector's map on every call
   (FeedbackVector::record, `through`): Splay's String + String helper records each call, chai's
   element helper each miss. A local record word per transformed pc, forwarding only new bits,
   takes Splay's cost from +0.96% to +0.25% and chai's from +0.76% to +0.51% (probe5's counts).
2. RayTrace's Class.create constructor, one function for all its classes, reads `initialize`
   through a megamorphic site; after it tiers up, the forwarder probes more ways a call. The
   forwarder's paths and their counts are identical with and without the tier-up.
3. Operator chains bake their reads' states and have no way back when one goes stale: every
   execution then replays the chain's ops through the generic helper. With both fallbacks, GBEmu
   still bails 4.6M times a run, and disabling property chains (TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_PROP_CHAIN=1)
   runs it 19.2% faster (Box2D 1.2%), while Richards, whose chains hold, would lose 0.6%. JSC
   counts exits and reoptimizes, SpiderMonkey counts bailouts and invalidates; so should we.

Proposed order: (C1) the chains' way back, which helps main's second stages now (GBEmu,
Box2D) and which the tier-up needs (more second stages carry more chains); then steps 4-5 of the
compact series; then (C2) the record filter and (C3) the tier-up at the last checkpoint on stable
feedback, measured again over C1. Each its own commit, measured against main. C2 is small; C3 is
probe2's function and the second-stage flag, once C1's slot and request exist.

WHAT THE EXEMPLARS DO

- When to tier up. JSC: Baseline to DFG at thresholdForOptimizeAfterWarmUp 1000 execution-counter
  units (OptionsList.h; calls and loop iterations), scaled by the code block's size
  (CodeBlock::optimizationThresholdScalingFactor: large blocks later, some never) and doubled per
  reoptimization (adjustedCounterValue, CodeBlock.cpp). SpiderMonkey: Baseline to Ion at
  normalIonWarmUpThreshold 1500, trial inlining at 500 (JitOptions.cpp). V8: Maglev at
  invocation_count_for_maglev 400 (1000 on Android), TurboFan at 3000, and never sooner than
  minimum_invocations_after_ic_update 500 after an IC changed: "How long to minimally wait after
  IC update before tier up" (flag-definitions.h). Our checkpoints come at about 100, 500, 2,100
  and 8,500 native runs; the last is past every exemplar's threshold.
- Who profiles. The lower tiers do: JSC's Baseline code writes its value profiles at each site
  (JITPropertyAccess.cpp, emit_op_get_by_id: emitValueProfilingSite), which the DFG reads when
  it compiles.
- A failed speculation. JSC counts its optimized code's OSR exits; past
  exitCountThresholdForReoptimization (osrExitCountForReoptimization 100, 5 from a loop, times
  the code type's multiplier, doubled per retry: adjustedExitCountThreshold) the code block is
  reoptimized with the exits' profile (CodeBlock::shouldReoptimizeNow, CodeBlock.cpp;
  OptionsList.h). SpiderMonkey: "Number of bailouts without invalidation before we set
  JSScript::hadFrequentBailouts and invalidate", frequentBailoutThreshold 10
  (JitOptions.cpp). V8 deoptimizes to its baseline tiers and reoptimizes later on the updated
  feedback.

1. SPLAY AND CHAI: RECORDS THROUGH THE TRANSFORMED MAP

A recompiled chunk's feedback vector is transformed (FeedbackVector::transformed, W4 step 7):
every record() goes through its RecordMap to the first-stage chunk's vector (map.target(pc),
that chunk, its vector, its record word: dependent loads and bounds checks), so a later
recompile sees the second stage's misses too. In the first stage a record is one load, an OR
and a compare. Two helpers record on paths that run every time:

- jit_add_strings (String + String after the template's tag guards) records the site's String
  operands and result on each call. Splay's GeneratePayloadTree concatenates
  `'String for key ' + tag + ' in leaf node'` for every leaf; after it tiers up, jit_add_strings
  takes 214 to 521 samples of 20K instructions (prof/splay-*), its hot instructions the map's
  loop (the record word's ORR and CMP after the vector's load, the back edge through `through`).
  The bytecode of both stages is the same 28 operations (TRUST_JS_JIT_DUMP).
- get_computed_element's record_element_miss records every element read outside the in-line
  set. chai's stringDistance reads `memo[strA.length][strB.length]` of holes and past the end
  (its Levenshtein memo, run for every "Did you mean" suggestion its proxy getter makes); after
  it tiers up, get_computed_element takes 3,617 more samples of 200K instructions (723M; the
  same map loop at its record).

Design: the transformed vector keeps its own record word per pc (the `record` it leaves unused
today) and forwards a record only when it adds bits. A record is an OR and nothing clears a
record word (FeedbackVector::record is their only writer), so a forwarded bit stays in the
baseline's word, and later recompiles see what they see today. The filter (probe5's
TRUST_JS_PROBE_RECFILTER; counts/probe5-*.txt, the usual counts, tier-up at 8,500 over the
fallbacks): Splay +0.96% to +0.25%, chai +0.76% to +0.51%, Djot +0.31% to +0.23%; nothing else
moves by more than 0.04%.

chai's remaining half: its assertion helpers' second stages (`flag`, the proxy getter,
`isProxyEnabled`, `Assertion`: +1,099, +1,488, +428 and +455 samples) are slower than their
compact first stages, and set_computed_element's named inserts grow (+565); stringDistance
itself costs the same in both stages (58,882 samples with its stubs against 57,500). Those
helpers' caches change as chai's proxies see new properties: V8's
minimum_invocations_after_ic_update case. Probe5 tiers up only at a checkpoint whose feedback
fingerprint is unchanged since the one before (the suppressed branch): chai +0.23%, Splay
-0.00%, Djot -0.07% (section 4's table).

2. RAYTRACE: THE CONSTRUCTOR FORWARDER

RayTrace's classes come from Class.create, whose constructor `function() {
this.initialize.apply(this, arguments); }` is one function for every class: one chunk, one
`initialize` read site and one forwarder-runtime cache for all of them.
construct_arguments_apply_forwarder elides the forwarding (and, for a field-list initializer,
the initializer itself) through that chunk's caches. Probe4's counts are the same with the
tier-up at 8,500 and without (332,643 calls: 273,119 elided initializers, 59,524 initializer
calls; the forwarder-runtime cache hit 154,004 times and re-derived 178,639, as classes take
turns in it). After the tier-up the calls run on the second stage's chunk (324,323 of them), and
the forwarder's instructions rise 8.5% (1,427 to 1,548 samples of 20K): the samples that grow
are in its inlined cache probe (try_ic_get's per-way shape tests and borrow releases), so a call
probes more ways of that site, which more classes share than it has ways. The rest of RayTrace's
+0.53% is its five recompiles. The forwarder-runtime cache's thrash (178,639 re-derivations in
332,643 calls) is main's too: a per-class entry would serve every class without the tier-up.

3. THE WAY BACK FROM A STALE BAKED SHAPE IN OPERATOR CHAINS

build_chain bakes a read's single cached state into its chain (ChainOp::LoadProp,
jit_cache_preferred). A guard failure bails: the chain spills and replays its remaining ops
through the generic helper, one call an op (emit_chain_marked's ladder). Nothing counts it, so
once the state is stale (a receiver class added later, a receiver whose shape moved on) every
execution pays two to four helper calls. On the fallbacks' build (879082db):

- GBEmu: 4,562,676 "data cached (other template guard)" reads a run, all chains'
  (`parentObj.LCDTicks < k`: a GetPropLocal, a Const and a Lt each through jit_exec); with
  property chains off, those and 13.8M more helper ops go (OPSTAT: Const 3.8M, GetPropLocal
  2.4M, GetPropThis 2.2M, Lt 1.6M, Gt 0.9M, Add 0.8M, BitAnd 0.7M ...).
- TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_PROP_CHAIN=1 against the same build (one run each, CPU 15; diag/nochain.txt):
  GBEmu -19.23%, Box2D -1.20%, DeltaBlue -0.09%, Djot -0.07%; Richards +0.62%, Crypto +0.10%,
  TypeScript +0.07%; the rest within 0.02%. The chains are worth keeping where they hold.

Design, after JSC's exit counting and SpiderMonkey's frequent-bailout invalidation:

- Count where the failure shows: a native read that reaches its helper and finds its site's
  cache holding the receiver's shape is a stale bake (PROPSTAT's "data cached (other template
  guard)"; with property chains off GBEmu has none). The JIT's property helpers (the chain's
  replay reaches the generic one) bump a per-chunk counter when their cache lookup hits a data
  way: no machine code changes, and with both fallbacks only a chain's replay gets there.
- Past 100 such hits a chunk (JSC's osrExitCountForReoptimization; SpiderMonkey uses 10
  bailouts), the chunk asks for one reoptimization: it re-arms its inline checkpoint, so the
  function's next call through the call helper recompiles it (compile_with_inlines from the
  current caches, the chunk's plan re-planned) with property chains off for that chunk
  (SpiderMonkey's hadFrequentBailouts: the recompile stops the speculation that failed). Its
  reads are today's template with the fallback, which a moved shape does not defeat.
- The new chunk goes into a third set-once slot (FunctionRuntime::code3, preferred by
  execution_code_for over code2 and code), with the call caches' epoch: a slot is never
  replaced, so raw `*const Rc<Chunk>` cache entries and running frames' leases stay valid, as
  for code2 today. One reoptimization a function: a second request is ignored, as JSC's retry
  counter and SpiderMonkey's invalidation limits bound theirs.
- A frame already running the bailing code keeps it to its end: the reoptimization serves
  later calls (no on-stack replacement into the new chunk). GBEmu's bailing chains are in second
  stages called again and again: its scanline handlers (LINECONTROL's `function (parentObj) {
  if (parentObj.LCDTicks < 80) ...`, gbemu-part2.js:5988) and executeIteration (5732), which
  run() calls each time (5703, 5712).
- Expected: GBEmu most of the 19.2% and Box2D its 1.2%, Richards keeping its chains (they do not
  fail); measured against main as its own commit.

4. THE TIER-UP AT THE LAST CHECKPOINT

At the checkpoint at or past 8,500 native runs whose plan is empty (or whose feedback is
unchanged), a first-stage chunk recompiles once: compile_with_inlines with an empty plan, the
second-stage flag set for a seeded recompile, installed as code2, the epoch moved (probe2's
probe_tier_up). Census at 8,500 (tierup/census-at8500): Vue 12, React 2, Djot 3, chai 44,
Richards 1, DeltaBlue 3, Crypto 2, RayTrace 5, EarleyBoyer 6, RegExp 2, Splay 2, NavierStokes 0,
PdfJS 13, Mandreel 25, GBEmu 36, CodeLoad 0, Box2D 35, zlib 2, TypeScript 89 functions; on
stable feedback only (tierup/census-at8500s) Vue 9, React 2, Djot 0, chai 9, Richards 1,
DeltaBlue 3, Crypto 1, RayTrace 5, EarleyBoyer 2, RegExp 2, Splay 1, PdfJS 7, Mandreel 9, GBEmu
35, Box2D 29, zlib 2, TypeScript 44. No later inline plan is lost at the last checkpoint, and
the recompiles are fewest.

Over the fallbacks (probe5, d293f04f: 879082db and the probes; counts/probe5-*.txt, against its
own no-tier-up run):

STEPS

C1 the chains' way back (the counter at the property helpers' cached hits, the request, code3,
property chains off on reoptimization; tests: a chain whose read's shape moves on reoptimizes
once and its reads stay native; one that holds keeps its chain). Then steps 4-5 (calls,
LoadLocal). Then C2 the record filter, and C3 the tier-up at the last checkpoint on stable
feedback, re-measured over C1. Each measured against main as the series' steps were (bytes,
counts, TRust's pages, the gate).

Decided (the coordinator's, 2026-11-05, as the note recommends): C1 first, the stale operator
chains counted per chunk in the property helpers (no machine-code change) and, past JSC's 100
exits, the function recompiled once with property chains off into a third set-once code slot,
the call caches' epoch bumped (JSC's exit counting and CodeBlock::shouldReoptimizeNow,
SpiderMonkey's bailout counting); its own commit against main. Then compact templates' steps 4
and 5, then C2 (a recompiled chunk's records forwarded only when they add bits) and C3 (the
tier-up at the last checkpoint, with V8's rule of waiting until feedback is stable), re-measured
on top of C1.

### JIT chains: the way back from a stale baked shape (C1, record, 2026-11-05)

63c80e0c on p2-c1, from main 0546c1fc (an agent's; landed by fast-forward): the tier-up design
note's C1, as decided. Two earlier
versions were measured on the way: fcceec26 cleared a bailing chunk's inline checkpoint before
the recompile, and kept it cleared when the recompile declined (now a declined recompile leaves
the checkpoint to run as it would have; none declined in any measured run); fcceec26 and
93219858 consulted code3 first on every execution-chunk lookup, which cost RayTrace about 0.06%
(now a function without a second stage takes its recompile in code2, and code3 is consulted
only after a second stage). The counts below are 63c80e0c's; the census and the controls are
the earlier versions', whose recompiles are the same.

An operator chain bakes its reads' and stores' single cached states (build_chain's LoadProp and
StoreProp) and replays its remaining operations through the generic helper when a guard fails.
The helper (jit_exec_inner) now counts, in a chunk whose native code built a property chain
(Chunk::property_chains, set by build_chain), each replayed GetPropThis, GetPropLocal,
SetPropThisDrop or SetPropLocalDrop whose site's cache holds the receiver's shape as a data
state (Chunk::note_chain_replay: the receiver's shape against the four ways, a depth of at most
3, no accessor or key-checked state; `prototype` excepted, whose deferred word takes the helper
once a function by design). No machine code changes. At 100 (STALE_CHAIN_REPLAYS: JSC's
osrExitCountForReoptimization, OptionsList.h; SpiderMonkey's frequentBailoutThreshold is 10,
JitOptions.cpp) the chunk asks once (Chunk::reoptimize) and re-arms its inline checkpoint to the
next native entry, where Interp::try_inline_recompile makes the recompile: plan_inlines over the
function's first-stage chunk and compile_with_inlines from its caches, as the inline recompile
is, with Chunk::no_property_chains set on the new chunk, so build_chain builds no property chain
in it. After a second stage the chunk lands in a third set-once slot, FunctionRuntime::code3,
which execution_code_for prefers (realm permitting) over code2; a function without a second
stage takes it in code2 (so a function without one never looks at code3); the call caches'
epoch moves, as a landed second stage's does. Frames running the bailing chunk finish in it. As JSC
reoptimizes a code block past its exit count (CodeBlock::shouldReoptimizeNow, CodeBlock.cpp)
and SpiderMonkey invalidates a script after frequentBailoutThreshold bailouts and sets
JSScript::hadFrequentBailouts. TRUST_JS_TIER_LOG=1 reports each recompile (its replays, inline
sites and bytecode compile time) or decline; TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_CHAIN_REOPTIMIZE=1 turns it off.

Test: jit::chain_reoptimize_tests (a warm engine bakes chains in five functions on one receiver
class: a local's read compared, `this`'s read masked, a store of a masked value, one that
keeps its class, and one whose inline checkpoint gives it a second stage first; read on a
second class, the three recompile once into code2 and the staged one into code3, each running
natively with no property chain, replaying nothing and computing the same; the fourth keeps
its chain). With TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_CHAIN_REOPTIMIZE=1 the test fails at its first recompile
check.

CallWithThis 21%. Decided (the coordinator's, 2026-11-05): the test change in 37ebcefa approved
(the failing root was a stale word in the call helper's frame, 16 bytes deeper with the shared

### Compact baseline templates, step 4: calls (record, 2026-11-05)

c64d9abc on p2-compact-s4b, from main e2ac4c7e (whose code is 63c80e0c's), after 37ebcefa (a test
fix, below): the design's item 5. The measurements are 9321681d's, whose engine code c64d9abc's is
(the rebase onto 37ebcefa changed only tests.rs).

A call site's template (Call, CallWithThis) tests its call cache's way 0 in line and, on a native
callee's hit, each intrinsic its arity can reach: CallWithThis(1)'s family already in a shared
stub outside loops (Intrinsics1), but Function.prototype.call (argc 1 to 8, 17 instructions) and
Array.prototype.pop (argc 0) in line at every site, then the direct call's stub, and the checked
helpers H_CALL_HIT and H_CALL open-coded (11 and 7 instructions). At a compact site
(compact_templates: first-stage code outside loops) the hit now enters one shared stub for every
intrinsic of the site's arity (SharedStub::IntrinsicCall { argc, array, function_call, discard }:
the one- and two-argument families, Math.max and Math.min, Array.prototype.pop,
Function.prototype.call), only for a native callee (the intrinsic id's test stays in line), with
the status return of the existing intrinsic stubs; and H_CALL_HIT, H_CALL and `new`'s H_NEW run
through their shared helper stubs (SharedStub::Helper, which passes x1 = pc | way << 16 on). The
callee's identity test, the direct sequence's stub call and the end poll stay in line. Second
stages and loop bodies keep today's templates.

V8's Sparkplug calls a Call builtin at every site (baseline-compiler.cc, BuildCall);
SpiderMonkey's Baseline attaches its call intrinsics (Function.prototype.call, Math.max) to the
call IC's stub chain; JSC's Baseline keeps the callee check of its call link in line and calls
shared thunks for the rest.

Test: jit::compact_call_tests calls each intrinsic at compact sites (completed, declined by a
non-object receiver or another argument type, throwing), plain natives, user callees (one site
polymorphic over five), uncached and non-callable callees and constructions, against the
tree-walker; tests/call-semantics.js is the same program for the release binary.

A TEST FIX FIRST (37ebcefa)

The lib suite failed one test with step 4, deterministically:
cross_realm_calls_keep_shared_intrinsic_tables_exact_across_collections, at the JIT tier, kept a
dead Realm alive ("false/false/false" for its three WeakRefs). TRUST_JS_GC_WHY=1 showed the only
root a native stack word in the generic call helper's frame (jit_call -> explicit_call, the call
of `$262.gc()`), naming the dead Realm's self-hosting environment (the private record of its
ToObject, LengthOfArrayLike, ... intrinsics); a collection from the host after the job
(Interp::gc_collect) reclaimed the Realm, and one with every site's H_CALL open-coded again
(a diagnostic switch, not committed) passed: the helper's frame sits 16 bytes deeper under the
shared helper stub's frame record, and one of its unwritten slots now meets a stale cell address.
The stack is scanned conservatively (Decision 0), which retains falsely, never unsoundly. A
deep stack scrub before the job did not help: the word is written within the job, before the
call.

The test asserted reclamation from a collection JavaScript requested; it now asserts it after a
host collection with no JavaScript frame on the stack (Interp::gc_collect, as the other
collection tests do), keeping the collections the cross-Realm calls request. V8's tests assert
collection with conservative stack scanning off (DisableConservativeStackScanningScopeForTesting)
and Oilpan's with no heap pointers on the stack (StackState::kNoHeapPointers). The fixed test
still fails when the Realm is kept (a global holding it: checked), and passes on main's code.

### Compact baseline templates, step 5: local reads without a dead TDZ test (record, 2026-11-05)

055f059a on p2-compact-s5 (b57534d0's tree, its message's figure corrected; the measurements and
checks are b57534d0's), from 07d3ad33 (the JIT map's attribution fix, below) over step 4
(c64d9abc): the design's item 6.

Every LoadLocal template tested its word for the TDZ marker (Empty) and carried the generic
helper's call with its end poll; a parameter or a `var` can never hold the marker. Each compile
now proves which reads find a value (Cfg::initialized_reads, a forward must-analysis over the
compile's CFG, jit_ir.rs): only Tdz puts the marker in a slot, every other write stores a value
(no operand word is Empty), and a read that did not throw leaves one (LoadLocal, GetPropLocal,
SetPropLocalDrop; StoreLocal, UpdateLocal and ResetSlots write); the evaluator projections copy a
binding back initialized exactly when it went in initialized. A fresh frame enters with every
slot a value; a borrowed frame's entry (a function OSR seeds its lexical slots from the parked
bindings, TDZ cells included), the catch and finally targets, the resumptions and the OSR
headers know nothing of a Tdz'd slot, and in a loop fragment, whose private homes arrive seeded
from parked bindings without a Tdz of their own, nothing of any slot it reads.

A proven read copies its word (ldr, str, add), in templates and in regions (whose tagged-home
read then emits nothing); the `LoadLocal; Pop` pair that guards a lexical's assignment emits
nothing. A read that keeps its test branches over its slow path, which it reaches only with the
marker in its slot and which therefore throws: the helper's call and a branch to the unwinder,
without the flag's test, the end poll, or the pair's second, unreachable call. The proof and the
new layout apply to every baseline site, loops and second stages included: a test that cannot
fail is not a size-for-speed trade, and the exemplars drop theirs in the front end, for every
tier. TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_TDZ_PROOF=1 keeps every test (DIAGNOSTICS.md).

The exemplars' front ends drop the same tests over less of the graph: V8's bytecode generator
remembers a variable's hole check for the rest of its basic block and keeps one checked on every
arm of a branch (bytecode-generator.cc, HoleCheckElisionScope, HoleCheckElisionMergeScope),
SpiderMonkey's emitter emits one CheckLexical a basic block (BytecodeEmitter.cpp, TDZCheckCache),
and JSC's bytecode generator lifts a variable's TDZ check once it is initialized in scope
(BytecodeGenerator.cpp, liftTDZCheckIfPossible); a test that stays calls the throw past it
(SpiderMonkey's emitUninitializedLexicalCheck, ThrowRuntimeLexicalError; JSC's emit_op_check_tdz
slow case).

Tests: jit_ir's analysis over straight-line code, branches, loops, catch targets, resumptions,
OSR entries, borrowed entries and fragments (three tests); jit::tdz_proof_tests runs reads before
and after their declarations in straight-line code, branches, loops (an OSR'd one), switch cases,
try/catch/finally, generators across yields, default parameters, classes, assignments,
destructuring and inlined callees against the tree-walker (tests/tdz-semantics.js is the same
program for the release binary). Treating every read as proven fails that test (branchTdz, sw1,
sw2-1, tc2-1, gen2, cl, asg, ...); dropping the fragment rule fails
function_tiering_tests::strict_private_fragments_publish_before_outer_author_cleanup.

THE JIT MAP'S ATTRIBUTION (07d3ad33)

opbytes.py counts a span holding a `region:` mark as region code. A region's operations take
their family through Asm::mark_op, which replaces the open families, and nothing closed it when
the region ended: a template emitted later in the chunk whose nested family closes (a helper
call's, a call's) resumed the region's last family, and its span counted as region code. In
Djot's map 907K bytes of baseline templates (of 2.14M) were counted as region spans, and the
per-operation template bytes lost every such site. Region emission now ends with the baseline
family; no machine code changes. Every templates figure in the design's census and the step
records 1-4 undercounts the templates by this; the machine code totals and the span diffs are
unaffected. Corrected figures, from fat-LTO builds with the fix (b0271a89 over the series base
a3fd64da, f92ac532 over main e2ac4c7e, 07d3ad33 over step 4; bytes-attr/, bytes-s5/):

### W6 step 6, part 1: large element blocks traced in chunks (record, 2026-11-05)

Why: the exit caps a slice at 1 ms but for the one that starts a cycle, and sustained
allocation's 1.97 ms slice (step 5's pause table) was one trace: its 200,000-word retained
array's block, which a trace reported whole.

What the exemplars do:
- V8 (main): an array larger than its largest regular object (128 KB) is marked in chunks of that
  size (MarkingProgressTracker::kChunkSize = kMaxRegularHeapObjectSize; only large objects use the
  tracker, src/heap/marking-progress-tracker.h:17-32). The visitor takes the next chunk, reposts
  the array while chunks remain and returns the chunk's bytes as its work
  (VisitFixedArrayWithProgressTracker, src/heap/marking-visitor-inl.h:618-687; the repost at
  658-665, the size at 673), which the step counts against its byte budget, reading its clock
  every 128 objects (src/heap/mark-compact.cc:2296, 2348-2370). The array stays black while
  chunked: the Dijkstra barrier greys a stored value, so a chunk is never rescanned
  (marking-progress-tracker.h:22-26); the tracker is reset at sweep (mark-compact.cc:5343, 6278).
- SpiderMonkey (main): no fixed chunk; the marker scans an elements range checking its budget at
  every value and pushes the rest of the range back when over (js/src/gc/Marking.cpp:1851-1858),
  reading the clock every 1000 steps (js/public/SliceBudget.h:66); a pushed range's start is kept
  valid across shifts (Marking.cpp:1660-1710). Its snapshot barrier needs no rescan either.
- JSC: a butterfly's elements are visited whole (runtime/JSObject.cpp:131-139); a re-greyed cell
  is rescanned whole.

Decisions (the coordinator, 2026-11-05):
- Fork 1, the chunk: V8's 128 KiB first, 32 KiB if sustained allocation's largest slice but the
  start's measured visibly past 1 ms. It did (below): 32 KiB (4,096 words) for the threshold, the
  chunk and the clock's interval.
- Fork 2, how a chunked block meets the cards: A, a take of the owner's card drops its progress
  and the block is traced again from its first chunk (JSC's whole rescan of a re-greyed cell,
  which the cycle does for every other cell; the card covers every mutation). B, rescanning the
  dirty runs below the progress, stays the post-W6 item (its measured value below).
- Fork 3, the accounting: element words count in a slice's bytes (8 each, as V8 counts a chunk),
  the clock is read every 4,096 such words, precleaning's small-round measure stays in cell
  bytes, and the whole block counts in the schedule's marked bytes at its first chunk (the
  cycle's live total).
- Under force (found by 436275e7's checks, below): F2, a preclean's pass begun at a forced
  slice's end leaves the cards of chunked blocks' owners set, for a pass begun out of work or the
  final pause to take; and a block's chunks there are 16 words or its eighth (8 chunks at most).
- mark_object asks the chunk window only for a block that keeps a record (Splay's +0.70% on the
  stop-the-world path, below), on a path of its own.

01accd72 (p2-w6-s6-chunks, on main 867ac484):
1. A cycle's drain (its slices and the final pause's drain) traces an element block of more than
   4,096 words 4,096 at a time (CHUNK_WORDS): the owner's trace reports its other edges and the
   chunk its block is at (GcSink::element_range, MarkSink::chunk_range); the drain records where
   the next chunk starts (Marker::chunked) and queues the owner again. A copy of the owner queued
   before shares the progress; one popped after the last chunk traces the owner's other edges and
   none of the words (CHUNK_DONE). The block's remembered record is committed after the last
   chunk: mark_object checks first whether the block keeps a record (Words::keeps_record), and
   only such an object takes mark_recorded_object (#[inline(never)]: the trace, then the commit
   unless the trace left words for a later chunk); every other object's mark is a tail call to
   its trace, without the frame the commit's check had made it keep.
2. A take of cards by an out-of-work preclean or the final pause forgets the progress of every
   owner it queues (Marker::restart_chunks). An ordinary cycle's precleans run only out of work,
   while no block is between its chunks (the owner's queued copy keeps the worklist from running
   out), so its restarts meet only blocks traced to their end; the final pause's meets blocks
   between chunks when a request, the margin or an explicit collection ends a cycle early.
3. Under force a chunk is 16 words (FORCED_CHUNK_WORDS), or a larger block's eighth
   (FORCED_MAX_CHUNKS = 8, as V8 queues an array at most 8 times at once, kMaxQueuedWorklistItems,
   src/heap/marking-visitor-inl.h:622), so that verification's cycles chunk most arrays in a few
   traces, and a pass begun at a forced slice's end (Cycle::forced_pass) leaves the cards of
   chunked blocks' owners set and drops their queued copies (Marker::keep_chunked_cards).
4. The element words a drain's traces report count in a slice's bytes, and the clock is read
   every 4,096 of them besides every 128 cells; the bytes a drain returns (a preclean round's
   measure, the log's `traced`) stay the cells'.
5. Stop-the-world markings (minor, major) and blocks of 4,096 words or fewer trace as before; the
   progress map is looked up only for a large block, on a cold path.
6. Tests (gc_cycle_tests): a_block_marked_in_chunks_keeps_what_is_stored_behind_its_chunks_in_
   every_tier (an On cycle with 4-cell slices, a test-only budget: objects stored behind a
   20,000-word block's chunks by an element write, a splice and an unshift are marked by the
   slices once an out-of-work preclean restarts the block; a last store that no slice follows
   survives the final pause through its take); a_forced_slices_preclean_leaves_a_chunked_blocks_
   card_for_the_final_pause_in_every_tier; a_forced_cycle_finishes_while_the_program_writes_a_
   chunked_block. Each piece removed in turn makes them fail:
   - the out-of-work preclean's restart: the slice-end barrier check ("traced cell (object) with
     a clean card holds an edge to unmarked cell");
   - the final pause's restart: its verifier ("marked cell (object) references unmarked"), in the
     new tests and in a_cycle_keeps_what_the_program_reaches... and a_weak_maps_entries_..., whose
     arrays force chunks at 16 words;
   - F2's kept cards: "the forced passes keep the card", and "the cycle's final pause ran on its
     own" (the livelock below).
7. DIAGNOSTICS.md describes the chunks, the budget and force's kept cards.

How force met chunked blocks: 436275e7 (16-word chunks under force, before F2) took 11,610 s for
its forced lib suite against e50f5725's 960 s (million_element_array_operations_succeed alone
timed out at 900 s under force; long_expression_chains_run took 804 s). Force's slices end with
the next 16 pages of a preclean's pass, which met blocks between their chunks, and a block
written at every safepoint was restarted at every pass: with 16-word chunks and 4-cell slices
its chunks never ended, the worklist never ran out, and the cycle marked until its margin forced
the final pause. Before chunking the block's re-trace was one cell, and the next drain ran out of
work. With F2 alone (307846a6) the cycles ended, but a block of a million words still took 65,536
traces, each one of a forced slice's 4 cells: million_element_array_operations_succeed ran past
8 minutes under force. With 8 chunks at most it takes 95 s (50 s with the cycle off), and the
forced suite 1,056 s (2ba32733; e50f5725's 960 s, 5504ace9's 1,158 s).

### W6 step 4's line of fixes: the margin and the external bytes (record, 2026-11-05)

A step 4 bug, cycles on only, found by the default-on lib suite (step 6):
external_memory_tests::replaced_maps_are_collected_as_their_tables_grow panicked at the debug
check every safepoint makes (value.rs:3493): "the poll words' heap bit disagrees with poll_due
(true)". Step 4's margin test, Heap::cycle_overshot (the heap's bytes, with the external bytes
still charged, past the byte budget by the cycle's margin), read the external bytes charged at
that moment from bytes_due, while Control::charge_external, which raises them, published nothing
during a cycle: the external budget waits for the final pause's sweep (step 4). A Map whose
tables grow by megabytes per few cells turned poll_due true with the heap bit clear; a release
could turn it false under a set bit. In release builds the final pause the margin asked for
waited until the next slice (64 KiB of cells later), however far the external bytes went past.
Force hid it: there collection_due is true while a cycle runs.

What V8 does: its overshoot test counts external memory in the global size it compares
(GlobalSizeOfObjects = old generation + embedder + external memory, src/heap/heap.cc:5324-5327;
AllocationLimitOvershotByLargeMargin, :5355-5385), and re-checks it as external memory grows:
every 128 KB of growth (kExternalAllocationLimitForInterrupt, src/heap/heap-controller.h:217),
UpdateExternalMemory finalizes a marking that overshot by a large margin at the charge
(heap.cc:6967-7020).

c2b046a7 (p2-w6-s6-margin, on the chunk commit 01accd72), approved as proposed: each refresh
during a cycle keeps the margin as two limits, the allocated bytes past which it is passed with
the external bytes charged then (Heap::cycle_overshoot_bytes, which bytes_due, so poll_due, and
the allocation check read) and the external bytes past which it is passed with the bytes allocated
then (the external ledger's cycle_limit); a charge past the latter sets the external `due` flag,
sticky until the sweep, and publishes it, as the external budget's does. poll_due then changes
only at a refresh, through allocation's slow path, or through a published flag, so neither a
charge nor a release can leave the bit and poll_due apart; due_work's finalize test stays exact
(the bytes allocated and charged now), so the safepoint after the crossing runs the final pause.

Tests: external_charges_past_the_margin_make_a_cycles_final_pause_due and
an_external_release_during_a_cycle_keeps_the_heap_bit_and_poll_due_agreeing (gc_core: a charge
within the margin, one past it, due_work's final pause; a refresh past it, then the release), and
a_maps_tables_grown_past_a_cycles_margin_bring_its_final_pause (gc_cycle_tests: a 300,000-entry
Map grown during an On cycle with a 2 MB margin; the final pause runs within the loop). With the
fix undone (bytes_due reading the bytes charged now, no publish at the charge) all three fail:
"the charge past the margin published its due", "a release leaves the heap bit and poll_due
agreeing", and the engine test the default-on suite's way, at value.rs:3493. With the fix,
external_memory_tests, gc_cycle_tests, gc_pacing_tests and gc_core's tests (132) pass with the
cycle off, on and forced, replaced_maps_are_collected_as_their_tables_grow among them with the
cycle on: it needed no pin.

Checks on c2b046a7 (a target dir of its own): those 132 tests ok with the cycle off, on and
forced; the fix undone, the three new tests fail as above; fmt and clippy x3 clean. The final
tree 3d6d4f60's chain and stage-end runs include it.

### W6 step 6, part 2: incremental marking on by default (record, 2026-11-05)

3d6d4f60 (p2-w6-s6-default-on, on the margin fix c2b046a7 and the chunks 01accd72):
TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL is on by default: the major collections the heap asks for on its own are
marked in cycles (V8's soft-limit start, slices of at most a millisecond, the final pause), and
TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=0 (or `off`) marks every major collection in one pause; `force` stays
verification's mode. A wasm32 build keeps it off: a slice's time needs a clock, which
wasm32-unknown-unknown lacks (std::time::Instant::now panics there; a cycle's start reads it),
as it lacks pacing (gc_pacing_enabled is not compiled there). A heap starts Off (gc_core's own
fixtures); the engine's heaps take the variable's mode in configure_heap. DIAGNOSTICS.md
describes the switch.

The default-mode lib suite (the cycle now on) on the first default-on tree found one failure:
external_memory_tests::replaced_maps_are_collected_as_their_tables_grow panicked at the poll
words' debug check, a step 4 bug of the cycle's margin (step 4's line of fixes, c2b046a7). With
it fixed the test passes with the cycle on and needed no pin. gc_scan_spike::
spike_scan_cost_is_linear_and_small failed once in that loaded suite and passed 3 of 3 alone: its
wall-clock bound joins the known load flakes (with a_thread_local_is_not_a_root and
payload_cell_tests::a_long_string_held_only_by_a_property_lives_and_dies_with_it).

### The tier-up's C2 and C3: the record filter, and hot first-stage code recompiled on stable feedback (record, 2026-11-05)

C2 landed on main over 3d2894b7 as 043948a1 (580b8e19's code plus W6's step 6, line for line; that
combined tree's ARM64 lib suite passed, 2,848 passed, 9 ignored, before main moved). C3 (702bc80c)
held, the coordinator's decision (2026-11-06): it costs Djot +0.26%, chai +0.41% and DeltaBlue
+0.25% beyond the 0.2% bound, and Djot is the phase exit's remaining gap; chai's cost first, as a
template fix (its second stages lose to its compact first stages in the proxy getter and the
direct-call stub), DeltaBlue's getters measured, then C3 re-measured, with V8's work-weighted
budget as the trigger's alternative if Djot's late tier-ups still cost.


580b8e19 (C2) and 702bc80c (C3) on p2-c2, from main 670b8d7a: the tier-up design note's last two
items, as decided ("C2 (a recompiled chunk's records forwarded only when they add bits) and C3
(the tier-up at the last checkpoint, with V8's rule of waiting until feedback is stable),
re-measured on top of C1").

C2, THE RECORD FILTER (580b8e19)

A transformed chunk's feedback vector (an inlined or recompiled chunk's, W4 step 7) sent every
record through its record map to the baseline site: the map's target, that chunk, its vector,
its record word, on every miss its helpers record, though the baseline's word already held the
bits (the note's part 1: Splay's String + String helper records each call, chai's element
helper each miss outside its in-line set). The transformed vector now keeps, in its own record
words (which it left unused), the bits it has forwarded for each operation, and forwards a
record only when it adds one (FeedbackVector::record). Nothing clears a record word (record is
their only writer), so a forwarded bit stays at the baseline site and a later recompile there
reads the same record; a record that adds nothing costs the first stage's load and compare. A
transformed chunk still reads no record of its own (record_word), its records being its baseline
sites'. No machine code changes.

Test: feedback_record_tests::a_transformed_site_forwards_each_new_bit_to_its_baseline_site (a
second stage's spliced Add misses on Strings three times, then on Booleans: both reach add's own
site); it fails when Boolean records are kept from the map.

C3, THE TIER-UP (702bc80c)

A first-stage chunk takes the compact templates outside loops, and only an inline recompile (a
non-empty inline plan at one of its four checkpoints, at about 100, 500, 2,100 and 8,500 native
runs) gave its function a second stage with the in-line templates: hot code with nothing to
splice ran on its compact first stage for good. At its last checkpoint, a first-stage chunk with
nothing to splice whose call caches hold the targets they held at the checkpoint before, and
whose function has no second stage, now recompiles once from its caches as a second stage
(Interp::tier_up; bytecode::compile_tier_up: compile_with_inlines with an empty plan,
Chunk::second_stage set before publication, now a Cell), installed as FunctionRuntime::code2
with the call caches' epoch moved, as a landed inline recompile is. Its records go through its
transformed vector to the first stage's sites, filtered by C2. Another Realm's call declines it.
So do a first stage that keeps the in-line templates (jit::compact_first_stage: x86-64's, or
ARM64's without shared stubs), which has nothing to leave, and a chunk whose constructions the
arguments-apply forwarder runs from its caches (construct_arguments_apply_forwarder: RayTrace's
Class.create constructor), whose native code the constructions do not run.
TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_TIER_UP=1 turns it off; TRUST_JS_TIER_LOG=1 reports each tier-up with its runs
and bytecode compile time (DIAGNOSTICS.md).

The stable feedback is the call caches' targets (each entry's callee, function and environment;
Chunk::call_targets), taken at each checkpoint beside the inline planner's fingerprint, which
also hashes each entry's epoch and code. Those move whenever any recompile in the process moves
the call caches' epoch (the epoch is a process static) or a callee gets new code: with the
planner's fingerprint, one function's recompile held the others back, and the first version of
this commit (df673e2e) failed its own test on x86-64, where the lib suite's concurrent tests
moved the epoch between the test's checkpoints. The probe's "stable feedback" column in the
design note (probe5) used that fingerprint, so it measured an epoch-dependent selection.

V8 waits for stable feedback before it optimizes (flag-definitions.h,
minimum_invocations_after_ic_update 500: "How long to minimally wait after IC update before tier
up"; Maglev at invocation_count_for_maglev 400, TurboFan at 3000); JSC's Baseline goes to the DFG
at thresholdForOptimizeAfterWarmUp 1000 (OptionsList.h) and SpiderMonkey's to Ion at
normalIonWarmUpThreshold 1500 (JitOptions.cpp): all before our last checkpoint.

Tests: jit::tier_up_tests (a function calling one native from a loop tiers up at its last
checkpoint, as a second stage whose records map to its first stage's sites, and its calls run
it; so does one whose cache refilled with its one target after the epoch moved between its last
two checkpoints, which fails when the tier-up reads only the planner's fingerprint; one whose call
site took a second callee between those checkpoints stays on its first stage, which fails when
the tier-up also takes a changed checkpoint's empty plan; a Prototype.js-style constructor the
forwarder runs stays on its first stage while the function constructing with it tiers up, which
fails without the forwarder's decline). On x86-64 the tests find no tier-up, as they should.

The forwarder's tier-up alone cost RayTrace a full point: the Class.create constructor, one
chunk for every class, whose constructions construct_arguments_apply_forwarder runs from the
chunk's caches (the design note's part 2), went to its second stage, while the four other
tier-ups (subtract, IntersectionInfo's initialize, two Color operations) gain 0.5%. The property
rule changes nothing that matters: the four workloads' stable property caches are not what costs
them. So 702bc80c declines the forwarder's chunk and a first stage with in-line templates, and
keeps the call-target rule.

What remains past the bound is Djot (+0.31%), DeltaBlue (+0.24%) and chai (+0.45%), from three,
three and 38 tier-ups:
- Djot's three (addMatch, a RegExp exec wrapper, skipSpace) compile 0.7 ms of native code
  (JIT compile 0.0451 to 0.0458 s), about 3M instructions of its 604M: the run ends before the
  second stages pay it back. DeltaBlue's three are one-line getters (`return this.elms.length`, a
  direction test) in a 257M run; their recompiles and the three epoch moves' cache refills
  (profile: Stub:CallSecondary, build_chain, the emitter) are the cost.
- chai's 38 (profile, the same binary with and without, c3/prof/chai-*): stringDistance's second
  stage comes out about even (its own code +2.64G instructions; the compact stubs it no longer
  calls -5.93G; the in-line paths' stubs and helpers, Intrinsics2, MinMax, Equal and
  get_computed_element, +3.11G), and the loss is in the proxy getter (+0.66G) and the direct
  calls' stub (+0.65G): its assertion helpers' second stages are slower than their compact first
  stages, as the design note's part 1 found.

getEol's loop, `for(;10!==(s=t.codePointAt(e))&&13!==s;)e++`, is one register region of 4,460
bytes holding 97.7% of the chunk's samples, spread evenly over about 190 instructions: about 180
instructions a character. Each iteration re-derives `codePointAt` from the string's prototype
(the tag dispatch, the realm's String.prototype, its shape and slot: about 50 instructions)
before the inline codePointAt, moves values through the operand stack in memory, and tests tags
at each StrictEq. A function's return costs too: ReturnUndef's epilogue restores d8-d15 and
x19-x22 and returns its frame to the pool.

COMPILE, THE TREE-WALKER, REGEX AND GC

- Compile (TRUST_JS_PERF_METRICS=1, the whole run, its counters' own overhead included: elapsed
  212 ms): 163 native compiles in 45.4 ms, 2.70 MB of code (16.6 KB a function, the largest
  132 KB), 106 inline attempts and 36 inlined; bytecode 9.6 ms, parsing 7.5 ms, lexing 5.4 ms. In
  the window the compilers are 6.9% of the cycles (about 6 ms at CPU 5); in the steady state
  0.4%. The known items: the tier threshold (t1a2, -9.5%) waits for TRust's page reuse, acyclic
  regions cost 2.1% (the compact agent's "regions only where a function has run"), C3's tier-up
  costs +0.26%.
- The tree-walker (a function's first 8 calls): 1.0% of the whole run (Interp::eval 0.62%,
  exec_stmt 0.12%, the rest under 0.1% each) and 0.5% of the window.
- Regex: the matching runs in native programs (Djot's patterns are sticky with indices, `yd`,
  RegExp:/.../dy in perf's map) and takes 0.3-0.4%; exec's runtime around the match takes
  5.3-5.9% (regexp_builtin_exec 0.83% itself, 4.9% with what it calls; regexp_exec_text_shared
  0.75%; regexp_exec 0.59%; the lastIndex slot 0.41%; the match array 0.31%). Djot's find
  (32659) sets lastIndex, takes a substring when it has an end, execs, then destructures each
  r.indices pair and takes a substring per capture.
- GC: 2.1-2.5%: 9 collections (8 minor, 1 major), 6.6 ms of pauses in the instrumented run.

CANDIDATES

Sizes are shares of the steady state's cycles (a pass is about 7.3 ms at CPU 5), the overhead
the candidate removes, not the work it keeps.

1. for-of steps in generated code. Size: the iteration machinery 2.9% itself (jit_iteration,
   Interp::iterator_step, try_intrinsic_iterator_step, inert_iterator_step,
   iterator_result_value's string-keyed reads of done and value), plus the Rust-to-JS call of
   each user iterator's next(): about 3-4.5% in all. IterStepL always calls the helper
   (H_ITERATION, jit_operations.rs:977-982; jit_iteration, bytecode.rs:26790), whose step runs
   the intrinsic array/Map/Set paths in Rust or calls next() from Rust and reads done and value
   by name (eval.rs:2045-2075). Djot's parse is a for-of over the block parser's event iterator
   (next at 19562, 65% of the steady state's cycles beneath that helper).
   - V8: for-of is bytecode: CallProperty next with a CallIC, then LoadNamedProperty done and
     value with LoadICs (src/interpreter/bytecode-generator.cc:3138-3153, 7685-7700), which
     Sparkplug compiles to calls of the Call and LoadIC baseline builtins
     (src/baseline/baseline-compiler.cc:1317-1330, 942-946); an array's next is the
     ArrayIteratorPrototypeNext builtin (src/builtins/builtins-array-gen.cc:1382).
   - SpiderMonkey: emitIteratorNext calls next and checks the result, then GetProp done and
     value (frontend/ForOfEmitter.cpp:145-175, BytecodeEmitter.cpp:2945-2975), each an IC in its
     baseline tier; packed arrays skip the protocol where OptimizeGetIterator holds (vm/Opcodes.h
     around 1451, jit/CacheIR.cpp:17263-17293).
   - JSC: op_iterator_next in the baseline JIT loads a fast array's or string's next element in
     line and otherwise calls next through its call IC and reads done and value through GetById
     caches (jit/JITCall.cpp:511-697).
   - Plan: (a) an array whose %ArrayIteratorPrototype%.next is intact steps in line (JSC's
     FastArray path), under the protector try_intrinsic_iterator_step already relies on; (b) a
     user iterator's next() goes through the direct-call sequence, and done and value through
     the property caches, as V8, SpiderMonkey and JSC do; (c) the helper stays for the rest
     (generators, Map and Set iterators first measured).
2. Calls to natives from generated code. Size: the boundary 1.4% itself (with_borrowed_values,
   call_native_committed_with, the agent's activation) plus most of jit_call_hit's 1.9%, for
   62,805 calls a run; the natives' own work is larger (exec 4.9% with what it calls, includes
   1.2%, substring 0.7%). A native callee declines the direct-call sequence at its first gate and
   takes the H_CALL_HIT helper, which decodes the op, consults the call IC and enters the native
   through the committed-call path (bytecode.rs:26071; jit.rs:9088-9213 for the intrinsics that
   do stay in line: charCodeAt and codePointAt, Array.isArray, push).
   - V8: these are JS-callable builtins that the call IC reaches without a C++ transition:
     StringPrototypeIncludes (src/builtins/string-includes.tq:10), StringPrototypeSubstring
     (string-substring.tq:8), RegExpPrototypeExec (regexp-exec.tq:31).
   - SpiderMonkey: CacheIR attaches includes, indexOf, codePointAt and the substring kernel in
     line (jit/CacheIR.cpp:8446-8475, 8477, 8375, 8107), Object.keys (10364), and calls any
     other native through a small exit frame (jit/BaselineCacheIRCompiler.cpp:2946,
     emitCallNativeShared).
   - JSC: host functions are entered through a native-call thunk from the call IC
     (jit/ThunkGenerators.cpp:431-518, nativeForGenerator and nativeCallGenerator).
   - Plan: (a) a native-call stub that enters a native's fast entry directly from the template
     (receiver and arguments where the template has them), keeping H_CALL_HIT for the rest;
     (b) includes, indexOf and substring in line where their operands allow, as codePointAt is.
3. RegExp exec's runtime. Size: 5.9%, around a match that takes 0.4%. Djot's 27,246 execs a run
   are sticky with indices.
   - V8: RegExpPrototypeExec builds the result from the match info in CSA
     (src/builtins/builtins-regexp-gen.cc:198, ConstructNewResultFromMatchInfo); indices go
     through a runtime call (src/runtime/runtime-regexp.cc:1020, Runtime_RegExpBuildIndices).
   - SpiderMonkey: exec is self-hosted, and its intrinsic exec runs a JIT stub that matches and
     builds the result (jit/CacheIR.cpp:7858-7944, GetOrCreateRegExpStub).
   - JSC: the matches array and its indices are built in C++ right after the match
     (runtime/RegExpMatchesArray.h:111-125; RegExpMatchesArray.cpp:92,
     createRegExpMatchesArrayWithGroupsOrIndices).
   - Plan: measure exec's fixed path piece by piece (argument and lastIndex handling, the legacy
     statics, the result's shape and the indices arrays), then cut what the exemplars skip: a
     result template with a cached shape, indices built with the result, no copy of the subject.
4. Generated code in Djot's scanning loops. Size: getEol and skipSpace are 6.6% of the steady
   state, 1.8x and 6.5x node-sp's time; their loops run about 180 instructions a character.
   - V8: Sparkplug's load of codePointAt goes to the LoadIC builtin, whose monomorphic handler
     for a string receiver checks the String map and the prototype chain's validity cell; the
     call goes to the builtin through the CallIC (baseline-compiler.cc:942-946, 1317-1330).
   - SpiderMonkey: CacheIR guards the receiver is a string and reads String.prototype's slot
     (GetPropIRGenerator::tryAttachPrimitive, jit/CacheIR.cpp:2647), and codePointAt itself is
     in line (8375).
   - JSC: get_by_id's baseline inline cache (jit/JITPropertyAccess.cpp:548) holds the string's
     prototype access once repatched.
   - Plan: GetMethod of a String.prototype native on a string receiver checked once against a
     protector of String.prototype's methods, fused with the in-line codePointAt; then the
     region's loop-carried values (t, e, s) kept in registers through the loop.
5. Calls and returns between JS functions. Size: the call and return templates are 5.1% of the
   steady state's operations and the call stubs 3.1%; ReturnUndef alone 2.0% (174 sites, 492
   bytes each). The epilogue restores d8-d15 in chunks whose regions use them, x19-x22, the frame
   pool and the context's slots. Plan: measure a call and a return in instructions against
   Sparkplug's (its frame is a push of the interpreter frame's registers and a stack check),
   then cut what a callee does not need (the FP saves of registers it does not write, the pool's
   bookkeeping).
6. String concatenation in the renderer. Size: about 2.3% (jit_add_strings, the in-place append,
   new flat strings), renderAstNodeDefault at 3.4x node-sp.
   - V8: StringAdd makes a ConsString for results of 13 characters or more
     (src/builtins/builtins-string-gen.cc:484-530; src/objects/string.h:1003-1029), and a
     substring of 13 or more a SlicedString (string.h:1115-1130).
   - SpiderMonkey: JSRope and dependent strings (vm/StringType.h).
   - JSC: JSRopeString (runtime/JSString.h).
   - Plan: measure the renderer's patterns first (an accumulator `e+=`, template literals); only
     then choose between ropes and the in-place append TRust has.
7. Smaller: computed-key method calls (the get_method_elem helper, 2.6% with what it calls),
   `new` through the helper (2.3% with what it calls; Djot makes an InlineParser for each
   paragraph and table cell), a RegExp object for each evaluation of a literal (0.6%; V8 clones a
   boilerplate, src/builtins/builtins-constructor-gen.cc:440).

Not candidates: the tree-walker (1% of the whole run) and GC (2.1-2.5%, its pauses W6's).

The order I'd take them in: 1 and 2 first, which are about calls leaving generated code and
together take roughly 6-8% of the steady state; then 4, which is 6.6% of the steady state in two
small functions and the pattern behind several more; 3 once exec is measured piece by piece. The
phase exit needs -12% of the window.

Decided (the coordinator's, 2026-11-06): candidates 1 (for-of steps in generated code: arrays
stepped in line under the existing protector, user iterators' next() through the direct-call
sequence and done/value through the property caches) and 2 (a native's fast entry entered directly
from generated code, includes, indexOf and substring in line as codePointAt is; one change serves
Vue's candidate 4 too) first, each its own step against main; then 4 (the scanning loops: a
String.prototype methods protector, the loop's values in registers); then 3 (RegExp exec's runtime,
measured piece by piece first). 5 and 6 after, measured.

### A function's new code picked up per callee, not through the global call-cache epoch (design note, 2026-11-06)

The coordinator's item after C3's findings: chai's C3 cost turned out to be the epoch's refills, not
its templates. This note designs how a function's new code can reach its callers without moving
CALL_IC_EPOCH. Nothing here is implemented: the owner decides whether it comes into P2. It is the
per-callee invalidation that Decision 27 carried to Phase 3 ("Carried to Phase 3", exit sites with
recompilation: "Each record moves the call caches' global epoch, so every call site in the program
re-resolves. The exemplars reach only the discarded code's callers").

How it was measured: a probe, p2-callee-probe 142d638c (not for landing). It is C3 rebased onto
main d5cb81ff (a7dda08d), plus the split's two modes from p2-c3-probe2 (bcae12f8, 96e0ef42), plus
diagnostics in builds with architecture-diagnostics (7e70950a, 142d638c). The diagnostics count
the direct sequences by form and record why each epoch move happened, with the refills each move
made. The probe ran in three modes: the tier-up off (main's behaviour), C3, and C3's epoch move
alone. Event counts come from one run each (target/p2/compact/callee/runs2). Instructions come from
the split's fat-LTO binary c9485a31 (counts/c3probe2.txt; counts/callee-epoch.txt for the
workloads the split left out).

Main's own direct-call count has a gap. TRUST_JS_JIT_CALLSTAT=2's direct count misses every shared
stub assembled before the first JIT entry reads the switch. The probe reads the switch first.
Main's count would leave out chai's 2.26M accessor and trap entries, and all but 3,598 of
Mandreel's 7.43M stub calls.

SUMMARY

1. Today every new code a function gets moves the epoch. An inline recompile, C1's recompile and
   C3's tier-up each put a chunk in a set-once slot and then move the epoch. The epoch is a process
   static, so every way in the process misses once and refills through Rust, in every heap. The
   old chunk stays valid, and only the function's own callers have new code to find.
   - On main, 99% of the refills after those moves fill the way with the code it already had:
     chai 23,464 of 23,545, TypeScript 64,653 of 65,182, Djot 3,700 of 3,735.
   - Each publication refills chai 350 ways, TypeScript 212 and Djot 103. About one of them finds
     new code.
   - Every move on main is such a publication except the FunctionRuntime drops (zlib's 31,
     CodeLoad's 39 and one of Gameboy's).
2. Estimated cost on main: the old code's refills times what a refill cost when C3's moves ran
   alone. That is chai 0.31%, Djot 0.84%, DeltaBlue 0.25%, TypeScript 0.13-0.25% and Box2D 0.15%.
   C3 would lose the epoch's share of its cost: chai +0.36%, Djot +0.15%, DeltaBlue +0.11%.
3. The exemplars reach only the callers. V8 and SpiderMonkey read the callee's current entry on
   every call. JSC relinks the replaced code block's incoming calls.
4. Three forms fit here:
   - (A1) A generation compare in the direct sequence: +2 instructions a call and +4 a
     construct. That is React +0.31%, EarleyBoyer +0.28%, Richards +0.16% and DeltaBlue +0.09% on
     main.
   - (A2) The old chunk's own request word. Both direct sequences already read this word at their
     retry gate. A replaced chunk asks every direct entry for the helper, which refills the way
     with the function's current code. It adds no instruction to the direct path and changes no
     template or stub.
   - (B) JSC's incoming lists. They add no instruction to the direct path, but every user-code
     fill must register, and chunk drops must clean up in both directions.
5. Proposed: A2. The epoch stays for what it fences: reclaimed code, dropped FunctionRuntimes,
   dead global environments, exhaustion and P3's watchpoints. It is also A2's fallback when
   another Realm still selects the old chunk. B remains the form for P3 if its invalidations,
   which concern incorrect code rather than old code, want exact unlinking: W4's dependency
   registry is its home.
6. Two side effects must be designed in, not assumed:
   - The planner's fingerprint hashes the epoch.
   - A call site's megamorphic and overflow-admission counts restart with each move. Gameboy's
     opcode dispatch depends on that restart: C3's 36 moves alone took 0.40% off its count, which
     is all of C3's Gameboy gain.
7. Open for C3: would the second stage win? Djot's three tier-ups gain nothing.

1. WHAT THE EPOCH DOES TODAY

CALL_IC_EPOCH (bytecode.rs:1222-1226) is recorded by every way at fill (CallIc::epoch). Every probe
compares it before trusting the way's raw pointers:
- In machine code: the call template's way 0 (emit_call_identity_way, jit.rs:10410); the shared
  CallSecondary stub's other ways, its code-keyed way and its overflow probe (emit_call_ways,
  10434); the construct probe (emit_direct_construct, 11466); and the property helper stub's
  getter, Proxy trap and setter calls (emit_get_prop_getter, emit_get_prop_trap and
  emit_set_prop_setter, 7883-8483).
- In Rust: Interp::resolve_cached_call_entry (interpreter.rs:15649), from which call_jit_cached
  serves Rust callers.
A hit enters the way's code through the direct sequence (emit_direct_sequence, jit.rs:10864), either
in line or through the process-wide DirectCall and DirectConstruct stubs. x86-64 has no direct
sequence: its calls go through the call helper.

It moves for two reasons:
- To fence pointers that are about to dangle. This is correctness. The moves are:
  - executable code reclaimed (Retirement::finish, jit_cache.rs:204);
  - a FunctionRuntime dropped, because code-keyed ways hold the addresses of its slots
    (function_runtime.rs:114);
  - a dead global environment's pin (interpreter.rs:14113);
  - P3's watchpoint sets (dependency.rs:87), whose only consumers today are tests.
  Exhaustion (u32::MAX) disables the raw caches for good.
- To publish new code. This is performance only. The moves are:
  - an inline recompile (code2, interpreter.rs:16412-16414);
  - C1's recompile (code3, or code2 for a function without a second stage; 16472);
  - C3's tier-up (code2, at the same point on p2-c2).
  A slot is set once and never replaced, and frames running the old chunk keep their lease. A way
  that keeps the old chunk therefore runs valid code. The move only makes callers re-resolve
  FunctionRuntime::execution_code_for (function_runtime.rs:84) so that they find the new chunk.
  The parked exit-site recompiles of region admission's step 3 moved it the same way.

Two other things read the epoch:
- The inline planner's fingerprint hashes each way's epoch (advance_inline_feedback,
  bytecode.rs:24196). Any move anywhere therefore changes every chunk's fingerprint once its ways
  refill. C3's call-target rule leaves the epoch out for that reason.
- A call site counts its megamorphic evictions, and its admissions to the overflow table, per epoch
  (counted_epoch, bytecode.rs:1380). CALL_SITE_MEGAMORPHIC_EVICTIONS says "the count starts again
  with each epoch", and an overflow admission budget of 64 is renewed with each move.

On main (the probe's tier-up-off mode), a refill is a fill that found a way for the same callee at
an older epoch. Refills are sorted by the moves in between:
- old code: every move in between was a publication, and the way gets the code it had;
- new code: the way gets new code;
- kept: a fencing move came in between.

| workload | publications: inline, C1 | fencing moves | fills | refills | old code | new code | kept | old code a publication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| chai | 67, 0 | 0 | 72,259 | 23,545 | 23,464 | 81 | 0 | 350 |
| TypeScript | 293, 12 | 0 | 71,654 | 65,182 | 64,653 | 529 | 0 | 212 |
| PdfJS | 18, 1 | 0 | 5,184 | 4,004 | 3,979 | 25 | 0 | 209 |
| Djot | 36, 0 | 0 | 4,705 | 3,735 | 3,700 | 35 | 0 | 103 |
| Box2D | 59, 3 | 0 | 7,240 | 6,281 | 6,208 | 73 | 0 | 100 |
| Mandreel | 16, 0 | 0 | 1,371 | 998 | 983 | 15 | 0 | 61 |
| Vue | 10, 0 | 0 | 1,372 | 550 | 534 | 16 | 0 | 53 |
| RayTrace | 11, 0 | 0 | 563 | 466 | 449 | 17 | 0 | 41 |
| Gameboy | 87, 46 | 1 | 6,436 | 5,257 | 5,020 | 67 | 170 | 38 |
| Crypto | 4, 0 | 0 | 213 | 111 | 105 | 6 | 0 | 26 |
| DeltaBlue | 23, 0 | 0 | 750 | 560 | 537 | 23 | 0 | 23 |
| EarleyBoyer | 20, 0 | 0 | 521 | 291 | 239 | 52 | 0 | 12 |
| Richards | 8, 0 | 0 | 97 | 70 | 64 | 6 | 0 | 8 |
| Splay | 8, 0 | 0 | 86 | 55 | 49 | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| React | 2, 0 | 0 | 24 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 0.5 |
| CodeLoad | 0 | 39 | 129 | 11 | 0 | 0 | 11 | - |
| zlib | 0 | 31 | 72 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | - |
| RegExp, NavierStokes | 0 | 0 | 1,242, 11 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | - |

So most of the call caches' fill traffic is refills after publications: 91% of TypeScript's fills,
79% of Djot's, 87% of Box2D's. About one way a publication finds new code. The census's 68 moves
for chai and 305 for TypeScript (C3's record, without the tier-up) are these publications. One
more difference: the epoch is a process static. In TRust, one page's or worker's recompiles make
every other page's caches refill too.

2. WHAT THE EXEMPLARS DO

- V8 keeps a function's current code in its dispatch-table entry. In its own words: "The
  entrypoint will always point to the current code of the function, thereby enabling seamless
  tiering" (src/sandbox/js-dispatch-table.h:28-31).
  - A call loads the function's dispatch handle, then the entry's entrypoint and parameter count:
    four loads and two address operations (MacroAssembler::CallJSFunction,
    src/codegen/arm64/macro-assembler-arm64.cc:2500-2510;
    LoadEntrypointAndParameterCountFromJSDispatchTable, 4169-4182).
  - A tier-up writes the entry (JSFunction::UpdateCodeImpl's SetCode,
    src/objects/js-function-inl.h:140-161).
  - Marking a function for tiering also goes through the entry: "Execute a tiering builtin
    instead of the actual code. Leaves the Code pointer untouched and changes only the
    entrypoint" (SetTieringRequest, js-dispatch-table.h:267-271).
- SpiderMonkey loads the callee script's jitCodeRaw on every call, with two dependent loads
  (MacroAssembler::loadJitCodeRaw, js/src/jit/MacroAssembler.cpp:4265-4276).
  - Baseline's call stubs do it (BaselineCacheIRCompiler::emitCallScriptedFunctionShared,
    jit/BaselineCacheIRCompiler.cpp:3352-3400).
  - So does Ion, even for a call to a known target (CodeGenerator::visitCallKnown,
    jit/CodeGenerator.cpp:7342).
  - Installing or discarding Ion code updates jitCodeRaw (JSScript::updateJitCodeRaw,
    vm/JSScript.cpp:3481-3505, from JitScript::setIonScriptImpl, jit/JitScript.cpp:695-713).
- JSC caches the callee and its code at the call site, as TRust does, and relinks only the replaced
  code's callers.
  - A monomorphic link registers its call site in the callee CodeBlock's incoming list
    (linkMonomorphicCall, bytecode/Repatch.cpp:84-107, linkIncomingCall at 102). The list is
    m_incomingCalls, an intrusive SentinelLinkedList (CodeBlock.h:980).
  - Installing new code walks the old block's list (ScriptExecutable::installCode,
    runtime/ScriptExecutable.cpp:213-214; CodeBlock::unlinkOrUpgradeIncomingCalls,
    bytecode/CodeBlock.cpp:2228-2239). A monomorphic link to the old block is upgraded in place
    to the new block's entry and joins the new block's list ("Upgrading Monomorphic DataIC with
    newCodeBlock", CallLinkInfo::unlinkOrUpgradeImpl, bytecode/CallLinkInfo.cpp:98-128). Any
    other link is unlinked.
  - Jettison and the block's destruction unlink the block's links (CodeBlock.cpp:2434, 940-948).
    A call site's destruction takes it off its list (~CallLinkInfoBase, CallLinkInfoBase.h:110-114).
    The collector unlinks links to dead callees (CallLinkInfo::reconcileWeakReferencesAtGCEnd,
    CallLinkInfo.cpp:174).

None of the three reaches call sites that do not call the function.

One difference matters here: whose "current code" it is. V8's dispatch handle belongs to a
closure's feedback cell, and SpiderMonkey's script belongs to one realm, so their current code is
per realm. TRust's FunctionRuntime is per heap and shared by Realms. A second stage with splices
belongs to its planning Realm (Chunk::inline_realm_compatible, bytecode.rs), so the current code
depends on the caller's Realm (execution_code_for(genv)). C3's publications are realm-neutral
(their plan is empty). Inline recompiles belong to their planning Realm, and so do C1's when their
plan splices.

V8, SpiderMonkey and WebKit main were fetched 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06
(target/p2/compact/exemplar-src/fetch-2026-11-05, -06b).

3. THE CANDIDATES

A1. A generation in the sequence (V8's and SpiderMonkey's read of the callee, as a check)
- Each chunk carries its function's code generation. A publication bumps it in each of the
  function's chunks (at most four).
- A way records the generation at fill, in CallIc's free word at 60, so the stride does not
  change.
- The [[Call]] sequence compares the two where it now tests the callee's inline-attempt byte
  (jit.rs:10945). A fill before the attempt records a generation that cannot match, so the
  attempt's one refill replaces the byte's test. The construct form adds the compare.
- Cost: +2 instructions a call (LDR, LDR, CMP, B.NE in place of LDRB, CBZ) and +4 a construct.
  That is +8 bytes in each in-line call sequence and +16 bytes in each in-line construct
  sequence. The shared stubs (DirectCall, DirectConstruct, and the property helper stub's accessor
  and trap calls) change once a process.
- Realms: a caller in another Realm refills to the old chunk at the new generation and then stays
  direct.

A2. The old chunk's request word (V8's tiering request, on the replaced code)
- Both direct sequences already read a word of the callee's chunk on every entry: the retry gate
  (jit.rs:10966-10978). The gate runs after every other fallback check and before any mutation.
  It sends the entry to the helper when the chunk's inline checkpoint is due (inline_retry_at is
  nonzero and the runs reach it).
- A publication marks the replaced chunk superseded and sets its word to 1, so every direct entry
  into it takes the helper (runs + 1 >= 1, and its run count stops there).
- The call-hit helper and the Op::New helper find the way's chunk superseded. They refill the way
  from execution_code_for and then make the call. resolve_cached_call_entry treats a superseded
  chunk as a miss for Rust callers. On x86-64, whose calls all go through the helper, A2 is this
  Rust check alone.
- No instruction is added to the direct path, and no template or stub changes. The in-line call
  and construct sequences, the DirectCall and DirectConstruct stubs and the accessor and trap calls
  all reach the gate already.
- Rust's inline machinery must leave a superseded chunk's word alone. Today
  try_inline_recompile's suppressed branch clears it once a second stage exists
  (interpreter.rs:16378-16382).
- A caller that misses the check runs the old chunk, which is valid. Correctness never depends on
  the word.
- Realms: when a caller's Realm still selects the superseded chunk (a second stage that another
  Realm planned), the helper un-supersedes it and moves the global epoch. That is today's
  behaviour, once for that chunk. A program with one Realm never takes this path.
- Like V8's request, A2 is a per-function word on the call path that redirects the next call. The
  difference is that TRust's callers cache the code, so the redirect also refills the caller's way.

B. JSC's incoming lists
- At fill, each way that holds a user chunk registers in that chunk's incoming list. The fill
  paths are CallSite::fill and store, the overflow table, and the construct, trap and callback
  caches. A way leaves the list when it is overwritten or refilled with another chunk.
- A publication walks the old chunk's list. A way whose Realm selects the new chunk is rewritten
  in place (chunk, chunk_raw, code, code_mem, pc_offs_ptr, n_slots and the direct flags) and moves
  to the new chunk's list. The other ways stay where they are.
- Nothing is added to the direct path, the callers never refill (so A2's new-code refills are
  saved too: chai 81, TypeScript 529), and Realms are handled exactly.
- A way is already rewritten today while frames that entered through it run: refills happen during
  calls, and call_jit_cached "runs from a copy". So the walk brings no new hazard into machine code.
- GC safety of the lists:
  - The lists hold the addresses of ways in chunk-owned call-cache arrays, which are boxed for the
    chunk's life. They are not GC cells, so there is nothing to trace or root and no barrier for
    W6's marking. They keep no chunk or callee alive: callee identity stays with the way's weak
    pin, and conservative scanning never sees them.
  - The hazards are drops, in both directions, as JSC's ~CodeBlock explains (CodeBlock.cpp:940-948).
    A caller chunk that dies first must take its ways off their callees' lists (JSC's
    ~CallLinkInfoBase). A callee chunk that dies first must empty its list first, so that no way
    later tries to leave a freed list. Today FunctionRuntime::drop's epoch move fences those ways.
  - Chunks die by Rc release, and a collection's sweep can start that, so the walks must allocate
    nothing and run no JS.
  - CallIc is Copy and gets copied, so the lists must name ways by address, not by a link stored
    inside the entry. Removal then needs an index per way or a search.
  - Chunks are !Sync, and the lists follow the caches' Cell discipline.
- Cost: a registration at each user-code fill (72,259 fills in chai, 71,654 in TypeScript), a list
  per chunk and an index per way. Every fill path must register. A missed registration only costs
  speed while the lists serve publications. If the lists replaced the epoch for reclaimed or
  invalidated code, a missed registration would be a correctness hole.

What stays on the epoch in all three forms: the fencing moves (reclaimed code, FunctionRuntime
drops, dead global environments' pins, exhaustion) and, until P3 decides, its watchpoints. For A2
it is also the multi-Realm fallback. On main that leaves zlib's 31 moves, CodeLoad's 39 and one of
Gameboy's. Every other workload goes to none.

Why A2 over B, beyond its size:
- The direct path costs the same in both.
- The refills A2 keeps (the new-code ones) are under 1% of today's refills.
- A2 adds nothing to fills and keeps no lists that two kinds of drop must maintain.
- A missed check costs the same in both, as long as the lists serve only publications.
- B is exact about Realms, but A2's fallback costs one move per chunk that another Realm still
  selects, and none in single-Realm programs.
- Both are grounded in an exemplar. A2 is V8's device on TRust's per-site caches. B is JSC's, and
  JSC's call caching is the closest to TRust's.
- Neither form makes the word or the lists a fence for incorrect code. P3's invalidations stay on
  the epoch until P3 designs them, where JSC's jettison form (B) is the natural one, as "Carried to
  Phase 3" already says.
