5. WHAT IT BUYS

On main today. The estimate is the old-code refills times what a refill cost when C3's moves ran
alone: the epoch-alone mode's instructions over its added refills. Where that mode also changed
compiles, an epoch move's cost is not its refills (see 6), so those rows use 1.2K instructions a
refill. 1.2K is the median of the workloads whose compiles did not change: Djot 1,368, DeltaBlue
1,178, Box2D 1,007, Vue 1,220, RayTrace 1,293, Richards 1,524, Crypto 850, Splay 1,071. chai keeps
its own 9,543, because its refills are Proxy reads through Rust (C3's findings: the extra Proxy
reads, GetProp and CallWithThis helper calls all go with the epoch).

| workload | old-code refills | instructions a refill | estimated saving | of main |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Djot | 3,700 | 1,368 | 5.1M | 0.84% |
| chai | 23,464 | 9,543 | 224M | 0.31% |
| DeltaBlue | 537 | 1,178 | 0.63M | 0.25% |
| TypeScript | 64,653 | 2,191 (1.2K) | 142M (78M) | 0.25% (0.13%) |
| Box2D | 6,208 | 1,007 | 6.3M | 0.15% |
| PdfJS | 3,979 | 1.2K (its own 8,503) | 4.8M | 0.07% |
| Richards | 64 | 1,524 | 0.10M | 0.07% |
| RayTrace | 449 | 1,293 | 0.58M | 0.06% |
| Vue | 534 | 1,220 | 0.65M | 0.05% |
| Gameboy | 5,020 | 1.2K | 6.0M | 0.04%, but see 6c |
| EarleyBoyer, Crypto, Mandreel, Splay, React | 239, 105, 983, 49, 1 | 1.2K | | under 0.02% |

These are estimates, not measurements. Main's moves come earlier than C3's, so each refills fewer
ways: Djot 103 per move against 210 for C3's. The estimate scales by refills, not by moves. The
implementation must measure the saving itself. Djot's 0.84% matters most, because Djot is the phase
exit's remaining gap.

For C3. The split (counts/c3probe2.txt; counts/callee-epoch.txt for the rest) takes the epoch's
share off C3's cost:
- chai +0.46% to +0.11%, Djot +0.31% to +0.16%, DeltaBlue +0.23% to +0.12%;
- React -4.89% to -5.00%, RayTrace -0.50% to -0.52%, Richards -0.22% (unchanged);
- against main's C3 counts (counts/c3c.txt, a different pair of binaries, so approximate): Vue
  -0.04% to -0.14%, TypeScript -1.70% to -1.78%, PdfJS -0.35% to -0.63%, EarleyBoyer -0.12% to
  -0.23%, Box2D +0.10% to +0.01%, Mandreel +0.10% (unchanged);
- Gameboy -0.32% to about +0.08%: its gain is the epoch's (6c).
That puts every workload inside the 0.2% bound. Djot still pays +0.16% for second stages that gain
nothing (7). C3's own moves refill chai 33,397 ways, of which 108 find the tiered-up code; DeltaBlue
235, of which 15; Djot 632, of which 12.

For P2's tier 1. Tier 1 ("region code only where a function has run", approved 2026-11-05) adds
the region spans by a recompile when hot. Each of those is a publication. Today each costs a
refill of every way that its function's callers did not need: 350 ways in chai, 212 in TypeScript,
103 in Djot and 100 in Box2D (section 1). At about 1.2K instructions a refill (chai 9.5K), that is
0.12M to 3.3M instructions a recompile, however small the function, and the other pages and
workers of the process refill their ways too. With per-callee pickup a recompile refills its own
callers' ways, about one. Tier 1's recompiles are then bounded by their compile cost alone, as the
exemplars' tier-ups are.

For Phase 3. This removes the second of the two reasons region admission's step 3 cost three times
what it saved: "Each record moves the call caches' global epoch" (Decision 27, "Carried to
Phase 3"). The first reason, recompiling code that has barely warmed up, stays with P3's
speculative tier.

6. SIDE EFFECTS THE DESIGN MUST HANDLE

A move does more than refill. The epoch-alone mode's other effects went both ways.

a. The planner's fingerprint. Every move changes every chunk's fingerprint, so the planner reruns
   at their next checkpoints. EarleyBoyer's three extra moves cost +3.4M (0.11%) with only 34 more
   refills, and its log shows two more empty plans. With per-callee pickup the fingerprint drops
   the epoch: chunk_raw already moves when a callee gets new code. C3's call-target rule then
   becomes the same as the fingerprint's.
b. What compiles read. Plans and templates read the ways' state. After React's two extra moves, one
   recompile spliced a larger body (101 operations and 17,984 bytes, against 77 and 12,444). That
   cost +0.33M, 0.11%, with three refills. Djot, DeltaBlue and Gameboy each had compiles that came
   out a few bytes different.
c. The eviction and admission windows. A site's megamorphic evictions and overflow admissions
   (64 an epoch, CALL_SITE_OVERFLOW_ADMISSIONS) restart with each move.
   - Gameboy's executeIteration (gbemu-part2.js:5732) calls through tables of hundreds of
     handlers: `this.memoryReader[this.programCounter](...)` (5751) and
     `this.OPCODE[opcodeToExecute](this)` (5762). Gameboy has three megamorphic sites, and each
     move renews their budget.
   - C3's 36 moves alone sent 72,147 fewer of the calls at two of executeIteration's sites through
     the call helper (pcs 216 and 68: 204,390 and 45,969 CallWithThis helper operations, against
     137,213 and 40,999; 67,536 fewer in all; callee/gb). That took 0.40% off Gameboy's count.
   - With per-callee pickup, Gameboy's epoch moves once a run. The budget then needs a renewal of
     its own: by the site's own misses, or a megamorphic path in machine code that reads the
     callee's current code, as the exemplars' generic calls do (V8's CallJSFunction for any
     function; SpiderMonkey's loadJitCodeRaw).
   - Megamorphic sites today: chai 7, TypeScript 9, Djot 5, Gameboy 3. Longer windows can make
     more of them. V8, SpiderMonkey and JSC do not reset their counts when another function tiers
     up.
   - Measure these sites and Gameboy with the implementation.

7. OPEN FOR C3: WOULD THE SECOND STAGE WIN?

Djot's three tier-ups (addMatch, a RegExp exec wrapper and skipSpace) run no faster in line than
compact (+0.10M), so whatever triggers them pays their recompiles (+0.14%) for nothing. React's
two gain 4.9%.

In V8 the answer is feedback-driven. V8 waits for stable feedback
(minimum_invocations_after_ic_update), and its optimizing tiers gain by speculating on that
feedback: Maglev's benefit comes from speculation, not from re-emitting the same operations.

Here a first-stage chunk and its second stage differ mostly in baked IC state. The in-line
templates bake each site's one cached state (a shape and slot, a call target, an intrinsic), where
the compact first stage reaches that state through a shared stub. So the question can be answered
from the chunk's caches before the recompile: how many of its executed sites hold a state the
in-line templates would bake. Sites that are megamorphic, uncached or native-bound (RegExp exec)
gain nothing.

Proposed measurement for C3's next step: the cache states at Djot's three sites and React's two,
to see whether such a count separates them.

8. STEPS, IF IT COMES INTO P2

1. A2 against main, its own commit:
   - The superseded state: a Rust flag, plus the retry word as the standing request. It is set at
     each publication (inline recompile, C1, and C3 once it lands) on the chunk the new one
     replaces in the Realms it serves.
   - The redirect in the call-hit helper, the Op::New helper and resolve_cached_call_entry.
   - The multi-Realm fallback.
   - The fingerprint without the epoch (6a).
   - The windows re-keyed off the epoch (6c).
   - Tests:
     - a caller of a recompiled function enters the new chunk at its next call, while another
       site's way keeps its epoch and does not refill;
     - a construct site picks up a constructor's new code;
     - a caller in another Realm keeps the old chunk and stays direct after one fallback;
     - a frame running the replaced chunk finishes in it;
     - Rust callers (a forEach callback, a Proxy trap through Rust) pick up new code;
     - a megamorphic dispatch site keeps its overflow entries.
2. Measured against main as the compact series was: counts, with Djot, chai, DeltaBlue, TypeScript
   and Gameboy against the estimates; fills, refills and megamorphic sites from the probe's
   diagnostics; bytes (no change expected); TRust's pages; the gate; and x86-64's checks on
   zombie.
3. C3 re-measured on top, with item 7 answered first.

Status (2026-11-06): the design is ready; its implementation in P2 pulls forward the per-callee
invalidation the owner's Decision 27 carried to Phase 3, so it waits on the owner's answer. The
coordinator recommends A2 in P2: on main it would remove most of the call caches' refills (about
0.84% of Djot, the phase exit's remaining gap, by the probe's estimate), and it unblocks C3 and the
approved tier 1 (region code only where a function has run), both of which arrive by recompile.

### Incremental marking crashes TRust's pages; its default reverted (record, 2026-11-06)

Found by the compact agent while it measured tier 1 on TRust's pages: TRust 78435d0's offline
replays on main 7dc412c8 (incremental marking on by default since b327786b) crash two of the three
pages. dom-reconcile aborts in jit_call with "a live weak target belongs to a known Agent heap"
(value.rs:5455); Vue TodoMVC segfaults with nothing on stderr; event-loop runs. Both crashing pages
run with TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=0 and on 702bc80c (before default-on). Neither the lib suite nor
Test262 (both run with the cycle on and under force) caught it, and W6's checks did not run TRust's
pages, which hold several Agent heaps in one process (target/p2/compact/census/pages/main7dc-*.err).
75f875b0 reverts b327786b, so incremental marking is off by default again (TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=1
turns it on; every part of the cycle stays); the GC test groups (gc_cycle, gc_core, external_memory,
gc_pacing: 146) pass. The W6 agent debugs it; default-on returns with the fix, a multi-Agent
regression test with a cycle open across agent switches and weak targets, and TRust's three replay
pages and spike with the cycle on in W6's checklist. Nothing with the cycle on by default was
pushed (origin/main 9deaece0).

### Two small fixes: CALLSTAT=2's shared stubs, the snapshot test's cache (record, 2026-11-06)

f9964bdb and 7e2d4153 (an agent's, p2-callstat-fix on main 7dc412c8), landed over 75f875b0 as
4e105bb1 and c26544b5. call_paths_enabled reads TRUST_JS_JIT_CALLSTAT on its first use, where it
was set only at the first JIT entry, after the first compile had assembled shared stubs without
their counters (direct calls counted: chai 23.59M to 25.88M, Vue 0.34M to 0.90M, Mandreel 0.86M to
8.29M). snapshot::tests::static_decode_validates_bodies_once_per_process retries at a fresh address
when other tests evicted its snapshot from the process-wide 16-entry list between its two decodes
(test builds count the evictions); the snapshot module passed 20 of 20 extra runs. Checks at
7e2d4153: lib 2,848 passed; clippy x3 and rustfmt clean; the gate's fixtures and difftest as the
base's; Test262 53,573 of 53,575, the two "no progress" timeouts of a saturated machine
(staging/sm/extensions/recursion.js, staging/sm/regress/regress-610026.js) passing on rerun. On main
after the revert: the snapshot and call-path tests (46) pass, rustfmt clean.

### Tier 1: region code only where a function has run (design note, 2026-11-06)

The owner's answer of 2026-11-05 (item 2) put tier 1 in P2: cheaper compiles, from the compact
templates (landed) and from region code only where a function has run, "a recompile when hot".
This note brings the census first: how much of the first stage is region code, on the fixtures and
on TRust's pages, and how much of it runs. Then it gives the exemplars' answer and a design that
assumes A2's per-callee pickup ("A function's new code picked up per callee"), with the cost if
the epoch stays instead.

Measured with a probe, p2-tier1-census (not for landing), from main 7dc412c8:
- e35d2c57, TRUST_JS_REGION_CENSUS=1: every native compile counts its entries and every published
  register region counts its entries in generated code (leaked counters). Both are printed at exit
  with the function's origin, the stage, the region's kind, its head pc, operations and bytes.
  The bytes are the region's own emission, its increment left out.
- 39b0ad49, for the counts: TRUST_JS_PROBE_HOT_ORIGINS names a list of functions, and the first
  stages of all other functions compile without acyclic regions (TRUST_JS_PROBE_DEFER=acyclic) or
  without any register region (=all). Second stages, borrowed frames (loop transfers, resumable
  bodies) and origin 0+0 keep theirs. The lists: a census run's functions with 100 or more native
  entries (an oracle, which knows each function's future), its functions with a second stage
  (another oracle), and none (every first stage: a design as it would be built).
Data and scripts are in target/p2/compact/census (runs/, pages/, hot/, second/, none/) and
target/p2/compact/scripts (census-*.py, census-runs.sh, census-pages.sh, oracle-*.sh).

SUMMARY

1. Region code is 21-50% of a first stage: Vue 30%, React 47%, Djot 28%, chai 29%, and on TRust's
   pages 25-30%. It is less of the whole than the plan assumed. Djot's region code in both stages
   is 24% of its 2.70 MB; the plan's 2.30 of 3.96 MB was the JIT map's attribution before 07d3ad33.
2. Almost every acyclic span runs. Spans start where calls go (pc 0), and fewer than 6% of
   acyclic bytes are never entered, 13% in TypeScript. What never runs is loops: 19-48% of loop
   bytes in eight workloads. What runs little is cold functions: most of chai's region code
   (823 KB of 1.16 MB), and 92% of the event-loop page's.
3. The exemplars' baselines emit no optimized code. Hot code tiers up by counted calls and loop
   iterations, loops enter the optimized code by OSR, and the optimizing tiers compile only what
   ran: code without feedback becomes an exit.
4. Measured before building (oracle counts):
   - Acyclic spans out of every first stage: every workload gains but zlib (+0.30%). Djot -2.00%,
     React -1.52%, Splay -1.09%, Richards -0.90%, DeltaBlue -0.82%, CodeLoad -0.72%.
   - This needs no recompile and no publication: second stages keep their spans.
   - Bytes: Djot 5.7% of its code, chai 17.2%, the pages 4.8-9.9% at t8.
5. A recompile when hot, as the plan put it, costs more than it saves on the benchmarks.
   - It recompiles whole functions at about 30 instructions a byte: Djot's 32 hot functions without
     a second stage are 1.3% of its run.
   - If the epoch stays, its publications refill the process: chai about 0.54%, Djot 0.75%.
   - The pages' cold code would gain from it: the event-loop page's 197 KB of cold-function
     regions. Item 4 takes the acyclic part of that (89 KB) without a recompile, and the loop part
     waits for item 6.
6. Loops are where the rest is: with loop regions out of first stages as well, five workloads gain
   2.2-2.7% in all. Loops are also where calls do not predict heat. Deferring loop regions costs zlib 42% and Gameboy 4.0%: those need back-edge counts and
   OSR, as in the exemplars. That step publishes, and it should follow A2.
7. Proposed:
   - (a) First stages without acyclic spans.
   - (b) Second stages' regions only where their spans ran (TypeScript's second stages hold 2.24 MB
     never entered).
   - (c) Then loops by back edges with OSR, after A2.
8. On the way: main crashes TRust's dom-reconcile and Vue TodoMVC pages with incremental marking on
   (the end of this note).

- Nearly every acyclic span runs. A function's first span starts at pc 0 (React's arrow helpers:
  entries equal to the function's, 219,992), and never-entered spans are under 6% of acyclic bytes
  except TypeScript's 12.9%.
- Loops are what never runs: 19-48% of loop bytes in Djot (27.6%), NavierStokes, PdfJS,
  Mandreel, Gameboy, CodeLoad, zlib and TypeScript.
- A cold function's loop can be hot. React's reducerBatch runs its first call in the tree-walker
  and moves into a borrowed frame at its loop (the first loop transfer). Its own compile is then
  entered once, and its inner loop region at pc 16 is entered 2,000 times: a function cold by
  calls and hot by iterations. RegExp's generated blocks are entered 23-29 times, each with loops.

What a recompile when hot would trade, by bytes. The cold functions' region bytes would not be
compiled. Each hot function with regions and no second stage today would be compiled again, all of
it (the functions with a second stage are recompiled anyway). The functions with deferred regions
would wait for their recompile:

2. WHAT THE EXEMPLARS DO

- Their baselines emit no optimized code. Sparkplug calls a builtin for each operation with
  feedback; a binary operation calls `<Name>_Generic_Baseline`, and its in-line Smi forms sit
  behind read-only flags (VISIT_TYPED_BINARY_OPERATION, baseline/baseline-compiler.cc:1269-1316).
  SpiderMonkey's Baseline calls the site's IC for arithmetic, comparisons and property access
  (emitBinaryArith: emitNextIC, jit/BaselineCodeGen.cpp:3035-3077). JSC's Baseline is a template
  JIT over its data ICs. None keeps a value in a register from one operation to the next, and none
  compiles a loop or a straight-line span as a unit. Register allocation over a function's
  control flow is Maglev's and TurboFan's, Ion's, and the DFG's and FTL's.
- Hot code tiers up by counted execution, and loop iterations count as calls do:
  - V8's interrupt budget is charged at each Return, by the bytecode the call ran
    (VisitReturn's profiling weight, baseline-compiler.cc:2905-2912), and at each JumpLoop
    (UpdateInterruptBudgetAndJumpToLabel, 2665-2671).
  - SpiderMonkey's warm-up counter is bumped in the prologue and at each LoopHead
    (emitWarmUpCounterIncrement, BaselineCodeGen.cpp:1665-1700, called at 7087 and from
    emit_LoopHead, 2590-2600).
  - JSC's execution counter is charged at op_enter and at each loop_hint
    (jit/JITOpcodes.cpp:1397, 1617-1619).
- A long-running loop enters the optimized code where it is, by OSR:
  - Sparkplug's JumpLoop checks the feedback vector's OSR urgency (baseline-compiler.cc:2640-2700).
    The TieringManager arms it once it has decided to tier up and the frame is still in a lower
    tier: "OSR kicks in only once we've previously decided to tier up, but we are still in a
    lower-tier frame (this implies a long-running loop)" (TieringManager::MaybeOptimizeFrame,
    execution/tiering-manager.cc:339-401).
  - SpiderMonkey's LoopHead compiles and enters Ion through IonCompileScriptForBaselineOSR
    (BaselineCodeGen.cpp:1755-1790).
  - JSC's loop_hint slow path calls operationOptimize and jumps to the OSR entry it returns
    (emitSlow_op_loop_hint, JITOpcodes.cpp:1622-1646).
- The optimizing tiers compile only what ran. Code with no feedback becomes an exit:
  - Maglev deopts unconditionally on a site whose hint is None (VisitUnaryOperation's
    kInsufficientTypeFeedbackForBinaryOperation, maglev/maglev-graph-builder.cc:1680-1686, and
    the same for binary operations, compares and named access at 2071, 2167, 2415, 3238).
  - Warp turns an IC with no stub into a bailout that always fires
    (WarpBuilder::buildBailoutForColdIC: MBail with BailoutKind::FirstExecution,
    jit/WarpBuilder.cpp:4185-4190).
  - The DFG gives up on a node with no prediction: "We have no information about what values
    this node generates. Give up on executing this code, since we're likely to do more damage
    than good" (getPrediction's ForceOSRExit, dfg/DFGByteCodeParser.cpp:1323-1332).
V8, SpiderMonkey and WebKit main were fetched 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06
(target/p2/compact/exemplar-src: fetch-2026-11-05, fetch-2026-11-06, -06c; sm/ and jsc/ from
2026-11-04).

  Splay -1.09%, React -1.52%, Richards -0.90%, DeltaBlue -0.82%, CodeLoad -0.72%, Crypto -0.66%.
  The functions that never get a second stage are better off without theirs too (the middle
  pair). The gains the plan's region table credits to acyclic spans (Richards 4.6%, Gameboy 2.9%,
  with regions off everywhere) are second stages': those keep their spans here.
- Loop regions out of first stages gain more where they run little (NavierStokes, CodeLoad,
  DeltaBlue, React, Djot: 2.2-2.7% in all) and lose where a loop runs hot in a function without a
  second stage (zlib +42%, Gameboy +4.0%, PdfJS +1.7%, Mandreel +1.2%), which calls do not
  predict (the cold oracle loses there too).

4. WHAT THE ORACLE LEAVES OUT

The oracle knows each function's future. A design that defers regions until a function is hot pays
three costs the oracle does not:
a. The recompile. A recompile at the first checkpoint compiles the whole function again, about 30
   instructions a byte, bytecode and native code. C3's split: Djot's three tier-ups cost 873,258
   instructions for 24,980 bytes, React's two 352,393 for 15,712. The hot functions with regions and
   no second stage today, at that rate: Djot's 32 (262,196 bytes) 1.3%, Box2D 0.47%, NavierStokes
   0.28%, DeltaBlue 0.25%, PdfJS 0.19%, Richards 0.13%, Gameboy 0.13%, Mandreel 0.12%, zlib 0.11%,
   the rest under 0.1%. On Djot that is more than the cold oracle's gain (-0.93%).
b. The wait. A hot function runs its first hundred calls without the regions it would have had.
c. The publication. With A2, a recompile refills its own callers' ways, about one. If the epoch
   stays, each publication refills every way in the process. The per-callee note's refills a
   publication, at its instructions a refill: chai's 117 publications cost about 0.54% (350 ways at
   9.5K), Djot's 32 about 0.75% (103 ways at 1.4K), Box2D's 64 0.15%, PdfJS's 39 0.14%,
   TypeScript's 106 0.05-0.09%, DeltaBlue's 6 0.06%, Vue's 8 0.04%. The other pages and workers of
   the process refill too.

5. THE DESIGN

a. Acyclic spans leave the first stage. A function's first native compile emits its templates and
   its loops' regions, and no acyclic span. Its acyclic spans come with its second stage: an inline
   recompile, C1's recompile, or C3's tier-up when it lands, where the exemplars put register
   allocation. This needs no recompile and no publication of its own.
   - Measured as built (every first stage, no list): Vue -0.25%, React -1.52%, Djot -2.00%, chai
     -0.13%, Richards -0.90%, DeltaBlue -0.82%, Crypto -0.66%, RayTrace -0.33%, Splay -1.09%,
     CodeLoad -0.72%, PdfJS -0.37%, Box2D -0.30%, TypeScript -0.30%, Mandreel -0.24%,
     NavierStokes -0.21%, Gameboy -0.11%, RegExp and EarleyBoyer -0.06%, zlib +0.30%.
   - zlib's loss is a hot function that never gets a second stage. Its two spans start at pc 0 and
     run on each of its 2,177,994 calls (origin 124312+1555; its inline plan stays empty). Hot
     first-stage code of that kind is what C3's tier-up recompiles (at 8,500 runs, on stable call
     targets), and its second stage would have the spans back. Without C3, a later checkpoint could
     recompile a hot function for its spans alone. Step 1 measures zlib with C3 and without it.
   - Even functions that never get a second stage run faster without their acyclic spans (the
     second oracle: React -1.50%, Djot -1.29%, Splay -1.08%, Crypto -0.59%, Richards -0.54%,
     PdfJS -0.52%), so not recompiling for them loses nothing. The exceptions are zlib (+0.30%)
     and EarleyBoyer (+0.01%).
   - Bytes (section 1): first-stage acyclic spans are Djot's 5.7% of all code, chai's 17.2%,
     Vue's 4.3%; on the pages at t8, the event-loop page's 9.9%, dom-reconcile's 7.8% and Vue
     TodoMVC's 4.8% (7.7%, 8.2% and 6.1% at t1a2).
b. Only spans that ran. A second stage emits a region only where its operations have run: their
   sites' caches filled, or their record words set. This is how Maglev, Warp and the DFG turn code
   that never ran into an exit (section 2). Second stages' regions never entered today: TypeScript
   2.24 MB (32.5% of its second stages' region bytes), Gameboy 361 KB (29.7%), PdfJS 194 KB
   (47.8%), Box2D 144 KB (13.3%), Djot 67 KB (24.4%), Vue 27 KB (58.8%).
c. Loops, by their back edges. Taking loop regions out of first stages is worth more: NavierStokes
   -2.1%, CodeLoad -2.3%, DeltaBlue -1.5 to -1.7%, React -0.7 to -2.1%, Djot -0.9 to -1.4%,
   Splay -1.1%. It loses in two places:
   - where a function cold by calls runs a hot loop (Gameboy +4.0%, PdfJS +1.8 to +2.6%, Mandreel
     +0.6 to +1.2%);
   - where a hot function gets no second stage (zlib +42%).
   A loop's own evidence has to decide, as in all three exemplars:
   - First-stage loops count their back edges into the function's budget. The tree-walker
     already charges back edges to the same budget (FunctionRuntime::tier_budget_spent).
   - Past the budget, the function recompiles with the loop's region.
   - The running frame enters the region at the loop head by OSR, or the next call does. A region
     is already entered from the frame's canonical state at its head. OSR also needs the new chunk
     to map the first stage's frame: its slots and the loop head's pc. C3's recompiles already
     carry a record map from their pcs to the first stage's; whether the slots match is to be
     checked.
   That recompile is a publication, and it gets its own design note after (a) and (b) are
   measured.
d. A2 or the epoch. Steps (a) and (b) publish nothing that is not published today, so they cost
   the same either way. Step (c)'s recompiles do publish. With A2, each refills its callers' ways,
   about one. With the epoch, each refills every way in the process, at 4c's rates: about 0.14M
   instructions a publication on Djot and 3.3M on chai. Step (c) therefore follows A2.

6. STEPS

1. (a), its own commit against main: first stages without acyclic spans. Measured as the compact
   series was: counts, bytes, TRust's pages (their compile time in a quiet window), and the gate.
   The expected counts are the "every first stage" column.
2. (b): second stages' regions only where their spans ran. Measured the same way. The bytes are the
   census's never-entered second-stage regions.
3. (c): a design note after A2: back-edge budgets in first-stage loops, the recompile, and OSR at
   the loop head.

### Incremental marking's crash on TRust's pages: a cycle's start dropped the weak collections it discovered (record, 2026-11-06)

THE CRASH

With incremental marking on, TRust 78435d0's replays crashed two of three pages on main
(the compact agent's runs; target/p2/compact/census/pages/main7dc-*.err). Reproduced with the
pure-main replay (target/p2/w6-fix/repro):
- dom-reconcile panics in jit_call ("a live weak target belongs to a known Agent heap", value.rs:5455).
  With TRUST_JS_GC_LOG=1 the same run instead throws "row.classList.toggle is not a function".
- Vue TodoMVC segfaults (the compact agent's run) or panics in Props::slot_of_key (an index of
  4.0e18 in an empty map: mine), reading a freed object's properties.
- event-loop runs: in a release build its heap stays below the cycle's 8 MiB, so no cycle starts.
  A debug build runs one there, and it fails as the others do.
- All three run with TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=0.
- It is not the JIT: the tree-walker fails too (TRUST_JS_TIER=interp: "cannot set property 'key'
  of undefined", from row.dataset).

A TRust build with debug assertions (target/p2/w6-fix/trust, TRUST_JS_GC_VERIFY=1,
TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=1) stops all three pages and the spike at the final pause's verification:

  marking cycle: weak collection 0x…: the entry under marked key 0x… holds an unmarked (Young)
  value 0x… after the final pause: a write its records missed

THE CAUSE

TRust keeps the internal slots of DOM wrappers in WeakMaps: js_platform.js's internalsFor, which
holds dataset, classList and the rest. The host roots those WeakMaps through embedder handles
(__platform_slots: HostState.platform_internals and the like).

A rooted weak collection is marked by the cycle's start, while it marks the roots (gc_core.rs
start_cycle). Then add_side_slot_owners fires the collection's side-slot owner edge at once
(try_fire: the owner is marked), with the start's client (Purpose::CycleStart). That client's
trace_side_slots discovers the collection (step 2b) in its own list.

A slice calls add_discovered_edges before its client goes. The start never did, and its client
was dropped with the list. So the collection's entries at the cycle's start were never registered
as ephemerons. The final pause reports only the entries written during the cycle, so it freed
every value that only an older entry held (DOM wrappers' internal-slot records). Their keys lived
on and read freed objects: the crash.

Only a collection already marked when the start registers the owners is affected. One the slices
reach is discovered by the slice's client, which reports it. The engine's tests kept their
WeakMaps in globals, which only slices trace. The final pause's verification would have named it
(above), but no test rooted a weak collection, and TRust's pages were not in W6's checks.

The other per-client state of the start survives:
- the Realm groups it activated (cycle_realms, saved);
- the homes, side slots and host graphs it traced, whose words it marks into the marker.

V8 has no such window (13.6, Node v24.22.2's deps/v8):
- Its start only marks the roots (src/heap/incremental-marking.cc:214-236, MarkRoots).
- An ephemeron table's entries are taken when the marking visitor visits the table
  (src/heap/marking-visitor-inl.h:641-690, VisitEphemeronHashTable). Entries with an unmarked key
  go to the weak-objects worklist, which persists across the steps (next_ephemerons_local).
- No per-step state is dropped. TRust JS's start fires the owner edges itself, so it must hand
  over what it discovered, as its slices do.

THE FIX

start_cycle registers the entries its client discovered, as a slice does (add_discovered_edges
after add_side_slot_owners). They wait in the marker and fire in the slices as their keys are
marked.

Tests (gc_cycle_tests.rs), each failing without the fix:
- a_weak_collection_marked_at_a_cycles_start_keeps_its_entries_in_every_tier: a WeakMap and a
  WeakSet rooted by an embedder handle (Ctx::handle), in every tier, through the cycle's own final
  pause (an explicit minor request, which collects no further). Without the fix it fails with the
  verifier's panic above.
- cycles_open_across_agent_switches_keep_each_heaps_weak_entries: two Agents on one thread, each
  with such a rooted collection. Each runs while the other's cycle is open, then both cycles are
  open. Afterwards the entries' values serve as WeakRef, FinalizationRegistry and WeakMap targets
  (observe_weak_target's heap lookup). Without the fix the test process aborts.

Single heap; not multi-Agent: one heap reproduces it, with no Agent switch. The second test covers
the switches the coordinator asked about.

### Tier 1 (a): first stages without acyclic spans (record, 2026-11-06)

### Tier 1 (b): second stages' regions only where their operations ran (record, 2026-11-06)

2b9008c0 on p2-tier1b, from (a)'s a8d07b73 (an agent's): the tier 1 design note's step (b).
- A second stage is compiled from the caches its first stage filled. compile_with_inlines seeds a
  named read's ways and a call site's targets, and a spliced callee's sites from the callee's own
  chunk.
- It now emits a register region (a loop or an acyclic span) only where those caches show that the
  region's operations ran before the recompile. A span holding a seeded read or call that is still
  empty never ran, and keeps its templates (jit::span_ran).
- Maglev, Warp and the DFG treat code without feedback the same way, as an exit: Maglev's
  insufficient-feedback deopt, Warp's FirstExecution bailout, the DFG's ForceOSRExit.
- A span holding no such site carries no evidence and keeps its region. Stores, updates, values
  and elements are no evidence: their seeds are cleared, or their in-line paths record nothing.
- First stages compile before any native run and keep their loops' regions.
- TRUST_JS_JIT_UNRUN_REGIONS=1 keeps the regions of spans that have not run (DIAGNOSTICS.md).
  Without seeds (TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_CACHE_SEED), the caches hold no evidence, and second stages keep
  every region.

Test: regions::stage_tests::second_stages_leave_out_regions_whose_code_has_not_run. A loop that ran
in none of its function's calls before the second stage runs as templates in that stage. The test
fails when second stages keep unrun regions: the loop then ran as a region 21 times.

### Per-callee code pickup (A2): a function's new code supersedes the chunk it replaces (record, 2026-11-06)

Landed by fast-forward: main ea6fd916 to 9747c2df (an agent's; gated on its own tree, below).
Decided (the coordinator's): EarleyBoyer's +0.38% is reported and taken with the series, a
net gain elsewhere (Djot -1.37%, Gameboy -1.23%, chai -0.35%, TypeScript -0.27%). Its cause is
the planner's: it splices only the closure a way names, and a way keeps the first closure of a
function it saw, while EarleyBoyer's parser makes its helpers afresh for each parse; main's epoch
moves refilled those ways by accident. Its fix is the exemplars' closure-call inlining, its own
step after candidate 2: the inlined callee guarded by its code, not its identity (JSC's
GetExecutable and CheckIsConstant, dfg/DFGByteCodeParser.cpp:1942-1951; V8's call feedback
widens from a JSFunction to its FeedbackCell for closures of one creation site, which TurboFan
inlines behind a closure check; SpiderMonkey's Warp guards the callee's script,
GuardFunctionScript). Not the probe's refresh of every way at each major collection: that moves
the epoch (or a per-heap one) for what the exemplars do with code identity.

The design note's A2 ("### A function's new code picked up per callee, not through the global
call-cache epoch", 7dc412c8), approved by the owner 2026-11-06 with Gameboy's admission budget
given a renewal of its own. One commit, p2-a2 9747c2df on main ea6fd916 (worktree
target/p2/compact/a2-wt). Measured against main ea6fd916 (fat LTO, lto/a2-main-ea6fd916 and
lto/a2-9747c2df); event counts from architecture-diagnostics builds (a2/ev2, a2/events-table.md).

WHAT CHANGED

- A publication (the inline recompile; C1's recompile without property chains; C3's tier-up when it
  lands) puts the new chunk in its set-once slot through FunctionRuntime::publish, which
  supersedes the chunk it replaces as the publishing Realm's current code (Chunk::supersede): the
  replaced chunk's retry word becomes 1, a standing request, so every direct entry into it takes
  the call-hit helper (its retry gate sees the checkpoint due); the chunk keeps the word it had for
  the time it is current again. No epoch move: no other call site re-resolves, in this heap or any
  other. V8's tiering request is the same device on a function's dispatch entry
  (SetTieringRequest, src/sandbox/js-dispatch-table.h:267-271); TRust's callers cache the code,
  so the redirect also refills the caller's way.
- The call-hit helper refills a superseded way in place with the function's current code in the
  way's Realm (bytecode::refill_superseded): the chunk fields Interp::call_jit_fast would record
  for the same callee, whose identity and proofs stay. A code-keyed way (another closure of the
  function) is refilled too, which a fill under the live closure's identity would leave behind.
  While the current code has no entry yet (not compiled), the generic call runs it.
- Rust's probes (resolve_cached_call_entry: the identity ways, the code-sharing retry, the
  overflow table) refill a superseded way or miss; a prepared call is stale once its chunk is
  superseded; call_compiled_target and the construct caches miss on a superseded chunk and refill.
- The multi-Realm fallback (bytecode::note_selected): a fill whose Realm still selects a
  superseded chunk (a second stage planned in another Realm) makes it current again and moves the
  epoch, so the publishing Realm's callers find the new chunk, as every publication did before.
  Once a chunk at most; none in any of the 19 workloads or TRust's three pages.
- The planner's fingerprint no longer hashes the epoch (note 6a).
- The overflow admissions (note 6c): an entry the table holds for a callee (stale or superseded)
  refills without an admission, and a megamorphic site's window renews after
  CALL_SITE_OVERFLOW_RENEWAL (1024) of its calls went through the full guards for want of an
  entry, as well as at an epoch move.
- Diagnostics: TRUST_JS_JIT_PUBLISH_EPOCH=1 moves the epoch at publications as before (no chunk
  is superseded); TRUST_JS_JIT_OVERFLOW_RENEWAL=<n>; architecture-diagnostics builds count
  supersessions, in-place refills, Realm fallbacks and renewals; CALLSTAT=2 counts the helper's
  generic calls for a superseded way.
- Tests (bytecode::callee_pickup_tests, 7); six fail with TRUST_JS_JIT_PUBLISH_EPOCH=1.

### A native's fast entry from generated code; includes, indexOf and substring in line (design note, 2026-11-06)

Decided (the coordinator's, under the owner's approval of design questions as recommended,
2026-11-04): A1 (the class test and the native's call in a machine-code stub, as SpiderMonkey's
and JSC's), B2 (the boundary keeps depth, the construct state, call_site, the pending tail and
the Agent restore, and drops the two interrupt polls and the safepoint at a native's entry, as
all three exemplars do, with the proposed tests that a deadline interrupts and an allocating
native's loop collects at its back edge), C1 (template ids of their own for includes, indexOf
and substring, as codePointAt's and charCodeAt's). Steps 1-3 as proposed, each measured before
the next.

Djot's candidate 2 in the coordinator's decided order (plan, "### Djot's gap, by where its time
goes", CANDIDATES 2 and "Decided"), which also serves Vue's candidate 4 (plan, "### Vue's native
calls, measured"). Nothing here is implemented. Census and microbenchmarks ran on the fat-LTO build
of tier 1 (b) (target/p2/compact/lto/t1b-2b9008c0), whose JIT is main ea6fd916's; the exemplars'
sources were fetched 2026-11-06 06:42Z (target/p2/compact/exemplar-src/fetch-2026-11-06d). Data:
target/p2/compact/c2/ (census-notes.txt, natstat/, natc.js, natb.js, per-iter-*.txt, split-*.txt).

SUMMARY

1. A native callee declines the direct-call sequence at its first gate and takes the call-hit
   helper (H_CALL_HIT), which decodes the call op, reads the way and either runs the native on the
   caller's window (the light classes: no author code for these operands) or through the
   native-call boundary (call_native_committed_with). Measured an iteration: a light native
   costs the helper about 160 instructions (Number.isInteger: 410 an iteration, the helper 39%);
   a boundary native about 75 in the helper and about 230 in the boundary (Object.getPrototypeOf:
   677 an iteration). The in-line template class (codePointAt) costs 236 an iteration in all.
2. Census (NATIVESTAT=1, H_CALL_HIT's native entries):
   - Djot: 62,805 native entries. Light (String's primitive class): includes 13,002,
     substring 11,043, trim 172, slice 69. Boundary: exec 27,246, test 5,011, keys 2,498,
     replace 2,110, assign 1,376, splice 152, split 69, join 57.
   - Vue: 386,430 native entries: WeakMap's and Map's get 245,079 (operand-only), Reflect.get
     78,629, Reflect.set 23,763 and Reflect.has 10,724 (answered on their operands), parseInt
     13,452 and Number 12,085 (light primitive-argument class), and 2,700 others.
   - React: none (869 helper entries, all user callees in warm-up).
3. What a direct entry removes, estimated from the split (a stub of about 45 instructions for a
   light native, about 105 with a lean boundary):
   - a light native: about 115 of the helper's 160. Djot's 24,286 light calls: 2.8M.
   - a boundary native: about 55 of the helper's 75 if the boundary stays whole (fork B1), about
     200 of its 305 if the boundary keeps only what re-entry needs (B2). Djot's 38,519 boundary
     calls: 2.1M (B1) or 7.7M (B2).
   - part (b), the generic native's own prologue for includes (ToString of the receiver, IsRegExp,
     position clamping: about 170) and substring (argument conversion: about 95): 3.2M for Djot's
     24,045 calls.
   Djot (582M on A2): 0.8% (B1) to 1.8% (B2) for (a), 0.55% for (b). Vue (1.39G): about 44M
   (3.2%) for (a), nearly all light.
4. The exemplars enter a native or builtin from baseline code with a frame record (the GC's and
   stack walker's view), an exception test, and a Realm switch only for a cross-Realm callee. None
   polls interrupts, counts depth or makes a safepoint at the native's entry; a native that recurses
   checks its own stack.
5. Proposed: (a) a process-wide native-call stub entered at a native way's hit, which tests the
   class's operand conditions in line and enters the native through one generic extern "C" shim,
   with a lean boundary for natives that can run author code; (b) includes, indexOf and substring
   as call templates with typed helpers, as codePointAt is. Forks in section 4.

2. WHAT THE EXEMPLARS DO

- SpiderMonkey. CallIRGenerator::tryAttachCallNative (CacheIR.cpp:14140) tries the inlinable
  natives first, then guards the callee's identity and emits callNativeFunction.
  BaselineCacheIRCompiler::emitCallNativeShared (BaselineCacheIRCompiler.cpp:2946-3058):
  - keeps: a stub frame and a native exit frame (callee, argc, frame descriptor, return address and
    frame pointer; enterFakeExitFrameForNative), which the GC and stack walks read; the arguments
    as vp (callee/result, this, args); the exception test (branchIfFalseBool to the exception
    label); a Realm switch only when the callee is in another Realm (isSameRealm);
  - drops: everything else. No interrupt check, no depth count, no stack check: a native that may
    recurse checks its own recursion limit.
  - In line: tryAttachStringIncludes (8446), tryAttachStringIndexOf (8477), the substring kernel
    (8107), codePointAt (8375), Object.keys (10364): guards on the callee, a string `this` and a
    string argument, then a typed VM call (CacheIRCompiler.cpp:5054, 5071: AutoCallVM of
    js::StringIncludes / js::StringIndexOf), with an exit frame and no JSNative vp.
- JavaScriptCore. A monomorphic call link caches the callee and its entry
  (linkMonomorphicCall, Repatch.cpp:84-107); a host function's entry is the native thunk
  (nativeForGenerator, ThunkGenerators.cpp:431-509). The caller lays down a JS call frame; the
  thunk stores it as vm.topCallFrame, calls the host function with its global object, and tests
  vm.exception. No interrupt or stack check in the thunk.
- V8. Sparkplug calls the Call builtin through a feedback-collecting trampoline
  (BaselineCompiler::BuildCall, baseline-compiler.cc:1717; CallReceiver, builtins-call-gen.cc:
  529-562), which enters the function's code (Generate_CallFunction, builtins-arm64.cc:2944-3023).
  String.prototype.includes and substring are Torque `javascript builtin`s (string-includes.tq:10,
  string-substring.tq:8): generated code on the JS calling convention, no C++ transition. A C++
  builtin goes through an adaptor and an exit frame (Generate_Adaptor, builtins-arm64.cc:54;
  BuiltinExitFrame, frames.h:948).

What all three keep: a frame record (GC and stack walks), the exception test, the callee's Realm.
What all three drop at a native's entry: interrupt polls, depth counting, safepoints. Re-entry
into JavaScript goes through the ordinary call path, whose callee checks the stack.

3. THE DESIGN

(a) The native-call stub.
- Entry. The call template's hit path tests the way's `native` word where a native now declines
  the direct sequence's static gates, and calls a process-wide shared stub, NativeCall{argc,
  with_this}, as the DirectCall stub is entered. The stub reads the way (x12) and the operands
  (x20): no immediates; ctx.interp for the interpreter's words (no heap or thread address, per
  "JIT shared stubs are process-wide").
- The light classes in line. The class byte (`CallIc::intrinsic`) selects the operand test that
  `native_operands` makes in Rust today (primitive receiver and arguments, Numbers, the
  operand-only collections); a pass enters the native through `jit_native_light` (below), and a
  fail returns to the H_CALL_HIT form, unchanged.
- The shim. One extern "C" function, `jit_native_entry(interp, native, this_slot, args, argc,
  out) -> u32`, calls the way's NativeFn at its Rust signature, writes the result word or places
  the error (`ctx.error`) and returns the flag. The stub retires the operands and pushes the
  result, as the helper does.
- The GC's view. The receiver, callee and arguments are the record's operands, which the collector
  scans whole while the record runs (jit::JitFrame); a call is a full frame effect, so a register
  region writes its values back before it (jit_regions.rs, frame_effect). The stub holds no Value
  in a register across the native. Nothing new to root; the native's own allocations follow the
  heap-held-value rule as today.
- Exceptions. As the helper: Err(value) becomes ctx.error and flag 1, and the site unwinds. The
  call's position goes into interp.call_site around the call (explicit_call's job today), read
  from the site as the DirectCall stub reads it (DirectCallSite::AfterReturn).
- The construct state. A native reads `constructing` and `new_target`; the stub enters only when
  the caller is not constructing and new.target is Undefined (the ordinary case, which the light
  path already tests), else the helper.
- The stack. The stub takes the direct sequence's depth gate (depth below direct_call_depth),
  which leaves the stack headroom the direct calls rely on; deeper calls take the helper and its
  stack growth.
- Re-entry (boundary natives: replace with a function argument, ToString's getters, Proxy traps):
  the native may run author code, so the stub enters through `jit_native_boundary`, which keeps
  what re-entry needs: depth (so nested calls count and the stack checkpoint fires), the construct
  state, interp.call_site, the pending tail (Function.prototype.call/apply hand their callee back
  through it), and the Agent restore where a native can switch Agents (with_host_callback). What it
  drops is fork B.
- Realms. The way proved the native same-Realm at fill (native_call_in_current_realm), as
  SpiderMonkey's isSameRealm; no switch.
- x86-64 has no direct sequence and keeps its calls on the generic helper; (a) is ARM64's, and
  the lean boundary of fork B serves both through the Rust helpers.

(b) includes, indexOf and substring in line.
- Three template classes beside codePointAt's: the call template tests the way's class, then a
  String receiver and a String argument (includes, indexOf with one argument) or Number arguments
  (substring), and calls a typed helper: `jit_string_includes(recv, search) -> bool`,
  `jit_string_index_of(recv, search) -> i32`, `jit_string_substring(interp, recv, start, end) ->
  word`. A miss takes the native-call stub. SpiderMonkey's attachments are the model (the guards,
  then a typed VM function); V8's are Torque builtins.
- The search helpers read two immutable string cells: no allocation, no author code, no
  boundary. substring allocates its result in the running heap (allocation does not collect in
  TRust; the next safepoint does).
- The classes: today these natives carry INTRINSIC_LIGHT_PRIMITIVE; the template ids replace it
  for the three, and their templates' misses keep the light test (fork C).

4. FORKS

A. Where the class test and the call live.
   A1. In the stub (machine code), with one extern "C" shim per native signature (proposed).
   A2. A leaner Rust helper only (H_CALL_NATIVE, the way's address passed in, no op decode).
   SpiderMonkey and JSC call the native from a stub built in machine code; V8's builtins are
   generated code. A1 removes the most (the helper's prologue, the Rust class match); A2 is
   smaller. Recommendation: A1.
B. What the boundary keeps for natives that can run author code.
   B1. Everything it does now, minus the decode (the shim calls call_native_committed_with).
   B2. What re-entry needs (depth, construct state, call_site, pending tail, the Agent restore for
       natives that can switch Agents); drop the two interrupt polls and the safepoint: the JIT's
       own polls at entries and back edges remain (jit::emit_interrupt_poll), as V8, SpiderMonkey
       and JSC poll in JavaScript code only.
   Recommendation: B2, with the dropped polls' tests (a deadline interrupts a loop of native calls
   at its back edge; an allocating native's loop collects at its back edge).
C. The in-line templates' class.
   C1. New template ids for includes, indexOf and substring; their misses run the light test in
       the stub (proposed).
   C2. Keep the light class and test for the three natives by builtin id in the stub.
   Recommendation: C1, as codePointAt and charCodeAt have their own ids.

5. STEPS

1. (a) for the light classes: the stub, the shim, the depth gate; tests: a light native at a
   site runs without the helper (a counter), its operands' non-light shapes take the helper, a
   throw unwinds with the call's position, a constructing caller takes the helper. Measured: the
   19 counts (Djot, Vue specifically), code bytes, TRust's three pages and the spike.
2. (a) for the boundary natives (fork B's answer); tests: replace's function argument, a Proxy
   trap and a getter re-enter; a tail call through Function.prototype.call; the interrupt and
   collection tests of B2. Measured as step 1.
3. (b) the three templates; tests: each template's hit and miss, ToString's order on an object
   receiver (the miss), substring's argument clamping. Measured as step 1, and Djot's elapsed time
   against node-sp in a quiet window under the HOLD protocol (the phase exit: 77 ms or less).

THE FAILURE

external_memory_tests::replaced_maps_are_collected_as_their_tables_grow, with pacing on and the
cycle on (e72e2168): "48513024 external bytes still charged after 30 replaced Maps" (the bound is
40 MB). It passes with the cycle off. It passed at d74d9c0b, where the cycle was off by default.

WHERE THE 48.5 MB IS

From the GC log (target/p2/w6-fix/extmem/maps-pacing-on.err, e72e2168, the test build):
- The loop charges about 6 MB of tables to the ledger per Map, and allocates about 192 bytes of
  cells.
- A cycle is open at the loop's end. Its start is the log's last event, after a minor collection
  that left 30.4 MB charged, past pacing's soft limit (the budget less the nursery's: 23.9 MB).
- None of the run's four cycles ran a slice: each ended with slices=1, its start. Only cells
  brought slices (one per 64 KiB), and each cycle allocated 576 to 1,152 bytes of cells.
- The 48.5 MB is the Map being filled and the Maps replaced since the last major's sweep, which
  left 15.2 MB charged. The minors freed none of them: each Map was live at a minor and was
  promoted.

The margin and pacing's budget:
- The budget is 25.9 MB, pacing's (V8's) limit after the last major: the 15.4 MB it kept, cells
  and ledger, plus V8's minimum step of 8 MiB, plus the nursery's 2 MiB (25,921,968 exactly).
- The margin is min(max(budget / 2, 32 MB), (maximum - budget) / 2): 32 MB, V8's
  kMarginForSmallHeaps.
- The margin counts the cells (0.24 MB) and the bytes charged (cycle_overshot). The final pause
  was due at 57.9 MB, 9.4 MB above the loop's end.

With fixed budgets, the unit tests' default, the test passed by the loop's phase alone:
- the cycles ran no slice either, and the minors saw up to 53.9 MB charged;
- the loop happened to end just after a final pause.

The bound in general, before the fix:
- During a cycle, only the margin bounded the charges.
- Payloads that charge the ledger: Map and Set tables, bound arguments, stack traces, internal
  slots.
- A program that allocates mostly such payloads kept its garbage until cells and charges passed
  the budget plus the margin: at least 32 MB over the budget.
- A program that stopped short of that kept its garbage until other allocation, or the host's
  idle advances, finished the cycle.

V8, IN CURRENT SOURCE

v8/v8 41b0e42f (main, 2026-11-05; target/p2/w6-fix/v8-src), with 13.6 (Node v24.22.2's deps/v8)
where it differs.

The ledger's payloads are V8 heap objects:
- A Map's or Set's table is an OrderedHashTable, a FixedArray (src/objects/ordered-hash-table.h:67;
  the collection's table, js-collection.h:24-27). It grows by allocating a new table
  (ordered-hash-table.cc:283-288).
- A bound function's arguments are a FixedArray (js-function.h:63-81). A stack trace's frames and
  internal slots are heap objects too.
- An object larger than half a page (128 KB: globals.h:770, build_config.h:80) is a large object
  of the old generation.

Their allocation steps marking:
- While marking, allocation observers step it every 64 KB of young allocation and every 256 KB of
  old (src/heap/incremental-marking.cc:54-55, 91-96).
- The observers watch every space, the large-object spaces among them (incremental-marking.cc:
  319-320; heap-allocator.cc:386-400).
- Each step marks the schedule's bytes within 5 ms (incremental-marking.cc:59-60, 723-745).
- A large object's allocation checks the margin first: past it the allocation fails and the heap
  collects, which finishes the cycle (large-spaces.cc:105-147; heap.cc:5490-5493).

External memory proper (Heap::UpdateExternalMemory, heap.cc:6959-7012):
- Its sources: ArrayBuffers and the embedders' ExternalMemoryAccounter (api.cc:12689-12697,
  9935-9948).
- It counts in the global size (heap.cc:5315-5318), so toward the global limit and the global
  margin.
- Every 128 KB of growth past the last check (heap-controller.h:219, heap-controller.cc:482-490):
  - with no cycle running, the start check (StartIncrementalMarkingIfAllocationLimitIsReached,
    heap.cc:1924-1962). Its limits (heap.cc:5592-5717): a soft limit, room below the old or global
    limit no larger than the new space's capacity, schedules the marking task; a hard limit, no
    room, starts marking now;
  - with a cycle running and its large margin passed (AllocationLimitOvershotByLargeMargin,
    heap.cc:5346-5377; the margins, heap-controller.h:158-187), a collection, which finishes it.
- Before both, at the heap's limit (ReachedHeapLimit): collections with retries, the last
  resort's (heap.cc:6993-6995, 1310-1345).
- No marking step comes from external memory in current V8.

The soft and hard limits:
- Current source has no ReportExternalMemoryPressure.
- Its successor in 13.6, Heap::HandleExternalMemoryInterrupt (heap.cc:1424-1475, called from
  api.cc:9690-9716), had them:
  - past the hard limit (the low since the last mark-compact plus half the maximum old
    generation, heap.h:612-615): a full collection that reduces memory, finishing a running cycle;
  - past the soft limit (that low plus 64 MB, heap.h:228, v8-internal.h:1014): start marking, or
    with a cycle running AdvanceAndFinalizeIfNecessary, a marking step per 128 KB interrupt that
    finishes a complete cycle.
- 13.6's flag external_memory_accounted_in_global_limit (off there, flag-definitions.h:2251-2253)
  is current main's only behaviour.
- The limits are still defined (heap.cc:1371-1383), but nothing in heap.cc or api.cc reads them.
  AdvanceAndFinalizeIfNecessary has no caller in the files read.

The critical path:
- A critical memory-pressure notification collects at once (CheckMemoryPressure,
  CollectGarbageOnMemoryPressure: heap.cc:3977-4028), finishing a running cycle.
- A moderate one starts marking only if none runs (heap.cc:3990-3996).

The memory reducer neither advances nor finishes a running cycle:
- Its timer may start a collection only while marking is stopped (memory-reducer.cc:84-87).
- Otherwise it waits another delay (196-218), and a mark-compact restarts the wait (219-222).
- The limit-based reducer returns while marking, and the mark-compact reschedules it (313-322).
- It samples the external counter (64-67), but its low-rate test reads only the young, old and
  embedder rates (heap.cc:3473-3503). The tables, being heap objects, count in those.

ArrayBuffers with a running cycle:
- Their backing stores are external memory as above (array-buffer-sweeper.cc:386, 397-400,
  454-466): they count toward the global margin and step nothing.
- While a cycle marks, no young collection runs for them (heap.cc:2834-2845).
- A failed backing-store allocation collects with retries (heap.cc:2850-2853).

TRUST JS AGAINST V8, AND THE FIX

TRust JS's schedule let the ledger's bytes overshoot beyond V8's policy:
- The ledger counted toward a cycle's margin (cycle_limit, as V8's large-margin check), but
  brought no slice.
- V8's allocation of the same payloads steps marking.
- This is not a design fork: the fix does what V8 does.

15c1d9ee: during a cycle, the bytes charged since the last slice count with the cells allocated
since it toward the next slice (SLICE_BYTES, 64 KiB):
- A charge past the ledger's slice_limit sets slice_due, and the poll words' heap bit, at once
  (Control::charge_external).
- The cells' threshold (cycle_slice_bytes) counts the charges a refresh saw. poll_due reads only
  stored thresholds, so the heap bit stays its mirror.
- Each part brings the slice by itself. Together, through the last refresh's thresholds, slices
  come at most 2 x SLICE_BYTES apart.
- The slice's budget (slice_bytes) counts the charges since the cycle's start with its cells
  toward half the room before the margin. The bytes charged at the start take their part of the
  room, as the margin counts them. The marking target stays the cells' bytes (marked_bytes).

One step serves cells and charges: the cells' 64 KiB, V8's young step. V8 steps old and large
allocations every 256 KB, so here a table larger than 128 KB brings slices about four times as
often as in V8. This follows the cells' existing single step.

After the fix, the new test's loop (below; Map by Map, the bytes charged after each):

| sizing | most charged | at the end | collections | the last cycle's slices |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fixed budgets | 13.9 MB | 6.9 MB | 66 | 6 |
| V8's (pacing) | 27.7 MB | 20.8 MB | 41-43 | 6-7 |

The original test passes with pacing on, its cycles marking in 6 or 7 slices
(target/p2/w6-fix/extmem/fix1).

Its 40 MB is not a one-pause expectation. With the slices driven as V8 drives marking, it holds in
both sizings with 12 to 26 MB to spare, so it stays.

Here pacing's budget is the bytes a major keeps (7.3 MB), plus V8's minimum step of 8 MiB, plus the
nursery's 2 MiB: 17.8 MB. The growing factor stays at its least, 1.1, because its allocation rate
counts promoted cells, a few hundred bytes per minor. V8's factor reads its old generation's
allocation rate (heap-controller.cc:245-252), and its global limit adds external memory at a factor
of its own (307-314).

Tests:
- external_memory_tests.rs, replaced_maps_are_collected_as_their_tables_grow_while_cycles_mark:
  - the loop with the cycle on (IncrementalMode::On), with fixed budgets and with V8's sizing;
  - one eval per Map, and after each, under 40 MB charged;
  - at least 10 collections, and the last cycle ran more slices than its start.
  - Without the fix: "48513024 external bytes still charged after 18 replaced Maps" with fixed
    budgets, and after 13 with V8's sizing.
- gc_core.rs:
  - a_cycles_external_charges_bring_its_slices: charges alone, a release, a slice's reset, cells
    and charges together;
  - a_slice_asks_the_bytes_behind_its_schedule_for_the_charges_too.
  - external_charges_past_the_margin_make_a_cycles_final_pause_due now expects a slice for a
    charge within the margin.

THE ARRAYS TEST (78191080, as approved)

replaced_arrays_are_collected_as_their_elements_grow pins the cycle off, so it does not depend on
W6:
- It failed with pacing on, here and on main: 8a9dc747, and the tier 1 landing gate's eed7110f.
- Its pattern 1 ran 8 collections against its bound of 10.

Each pattern on the release CLI (e72e2168, TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=0;
target/p2/w6-fix/extmem/arrays):

| pattern | fixed budgets: collections, most held | V8's sizing: collections, most held |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 40 x new Array(100000).fill(i) | 14, 9.0 MB | 8, 6.6 MB |
| 40 chained map over 100,000 | 51, 9.1 MB | 11, 15.4 MB |
| 400 arrays grown by push to 10,000 | 62, 8.4 MB | 32, 7.4 MB |

- ">= 10 collections" was a fixed-budget expectation. A fixed 2 MiB nursery collects about every
  2 MB of elements.
- Under V8's sizing the nursery grows from 2 MiB toward 32 MiB, since each minor finds the live
  array's 800 KB surviving. Pattern 1 collects about every 4 MB.
- "held < 48 MB" holds in both sizings: the replaced arrays do not pile up. That is the property.

The test now:
- runs each pattern in four evaluations and samples the nursery's budget between them;
- asks at least 32 MB / (the largest budget + 800 KB) - 1 collections. At most a budget and an
  array are allocated between two collections, before the first and after the last. That is 10
  with the fixed 2 MiB nursery, as before;
- keeps "held < 48 MB".

The test's engine (collections; the largest nursery; the bound; cells held at the end):

| pattern | fixed budgets | V8's sizing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fill | 14; 2 MiB; 10; 2.6 MB | 8; 4 MiB; 5; 7.4 MB |
| map | 51; 2 MiB; 10; 6.7 MB | 12; 16 MiB; 0; 21.9 MB |
| push | 62; 2 MiB; 10; 6.4 MB | 33; 8 MiB; 2; 8.7 MB |

Under V8's sizing the map pattern's bound is empty: its nursery reaches 16 MiB, half its elements.
A regression that stopped counting elements would still fail the fill and push patterns (bounds
5 and 2), and all three with fixed budgets.

OBSERVATIONS (not changed)

- The memory reducer. Engine::run_memory_reducer's can_start ignores a running cycle:
  - with one running, the reducer's start (Run) takes that cycle as its collection, because
    gc_start_cycle_for_host returns true when one runs;
  - that cycle's final pause then reduces memory.
  - V8's reducer waits instead (above). Passing can_start && !cycle_running would match it.
- ArrayBuffer data (BufferPressure) is outside a cycle's margin, which counts the cells and the
  ledger:
  - 64 MiB of new buffer data since the last major asks a major collection;
  - with a cycle running, that is its final pause at once.
  - V8 counts the buffers in the global size, toward the global margin.
- Two more of pacing's inputs see cells only: the memory reducer's low-rate test (Pacing::sample)
  and the growing factor's old-generation allocation rate. In V8 the ledger's payloads are heap
  allocation, so both count them. A program that allocates mostly such payloads looks quiet to
  both here. The same question as the slices': a design question for later.

The coordinator's dispositions: the memory reducer waiting while a cycle marks, as V8's does,
goes to the phase-end follow-ups; the ledger in pacing's growth factor and low-rate test is a
design question for later; the ArrayBuffer data outside the cycle's margin is noted.

GATE

WHAT CHANGED

A synchronous for-of step is ForIn/OfBodyEvaluation's step 6 (ECMA-262 e28783d5,
spec.html:23038-23043). The bytecode compiler (Compiler::emit_for_of_step) emits it in two forms;
IterNextBuiltin, a new operation, chooses one at each step by whether the loop's next method is a
built-in function (ObjectKind::Native):

- A built-in next steps through IterStepL, as every step did before: the intrinsic Array, String,
  Map and Set steps run without a call, other built-ins (generators among them) are called from
  Rust. This keeps the plan's (c): the helper stays for the rest.
- Any other next takes the generic sequence V8 and SpiderMonkey emit:
  - V8: src/interpreter/bytecode-generator.cc:3138-3153, 7685-7700.
  - SpiderMonkey: frontend/ForOfEmitter.cpp:145-175, BytecodeEmitter.cpp:2945-2975.
  - The sequence:
    - LoadLocal iterator, LoadLocal next, CallWithThis(0) with its own call cache (the
      direct-call sequence in generated code);
    - RequireIterResult (new: step 6.c's TypeError; an Object tag test in generated code);
    - Dup, GetProp "done" with its own property cache, Not, JumpIfFalse(exit);
    - GetProp "value" with its own property cache, then the body.
- As before, none of it runs inside the body's handler, so an abrupt step closes nothing; the
  body's handler and the IteratorClose pads are unchanged.

ARM64 fuses the dispatch with the step (jit.rs; jit_operations.rs emit_for_of_step):

- A next that is not a built-in branches to the generic sequence.
- An Array steps in line, as JSC's Baseline steps a fast array (jit/JITCall.cpp:511-697,
  emit_op_iterator_next). The template checks:
  - next's behaviour is %ArrayIteratorPrototype%.next (the identity test that
    try_intrinsic_iterator_step makes);
  - the iterator is an Array Iterator over values on an ordinary Array (ic_plain);
  - the element at its index is present below the used words.
  It advances the index (an integer: no barrier) and goes to the body with the element.
- %ArrayIteratorPrototype%.next (spec.html:42038-42070) runs no code on this path: an ordinary
  Array's length is a data property and an own data element's Get calls nothing, so reading
  the element before advancing the index is unobservable.
- Anything else, exhaustion included (it reads the length and clears the target), takes the
  helper's step unchanged.

The unfixed operations have templates of their own, for regions and other layouts. x86-64 has
templates for IterNextBuiltin and RequireIterResult and keeps IterStepL in its exec helper (it has
no in-line element reads).

A correction to the census's plan: the Array step relies on the next method's identity, not on a
protector. ArrayIterationProof (the protector) is GetIter's and IteratorClose's: it decides which
next the loop gets.

The VM and the exact-PC executor run the two new operations out of their dispatch
(vm_for_of_step_operation, jit_for_of_step_operation, #[inline(never)]). As two arms of
run_vm_inner's match they changed how fat LTO compiled the loop: 6.4 KB smaller, the same 223 call
targets, 1,607 fewer instructions, and the bytecode tier 0.4-0.8% slower on code that never runs
them (counts at --tier=bytecode: Richards +0.76%, DeltaBlue +0.66%, sa +0.55%; sa +0.14% at
--tier=jit). Bisected:
- the arms alone (no lowering, no JIT change) reproduce it;
- the arms last in the match, and the operations last in Op, do not help;
- out of line, the loop is back to 123,696 bytes (main 124,060), and the bytecode tier to
  Richards +0.08%, DeltaBlue +0.14%, sa +0.04%.

Ablations (DIAGNOSTICS.md):
- TRUST_JS_FOR_OF_STEP=helper keeps every step in IterStepL;
- TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_ITER_STEP=1 keeps the Array step in the helper.

Tests (iterator_result_tests.rs), with Node v24's answers, in the tree-walker, the VM and the JIT:
- the generic step: getter order and value's laziness at done, done's truthiness, non-Object
  results, abrupt next, done and value (none closes), body throws and returns, breaks (a close
  whose result is not an Object), a captured next, Proxy results;
- one site seeing seven kinds of iterator, generators around both forms, labeled continue;
- the Array step's edges: an exhausted iterator, holes, prototype elements, truncation, growth,
  frozen arrays, next replaced mid-loop and replaced before;
- the Array step in line (only the exhausting step reaches the helper), user iterators never in
  the helper;
- top-level loops in compiled fragments, closing.
