### Djot's gap, candidate 4: the scanning loops (design note, 2026-11-06)

Decided (the coordinator's, under the owner's approval of design questions as recommended):
fork 1 (a), String.prototype's ObjectFuse, two-level as SpiderMonkey's (vm/ObjectFuse.h's SMDOC;
CacheIR's GuardObjectFuseProperty, which Warp turns into an invalidation dependency), with
SpiderMonkey's semantics: a generation bumped by a tracked property's removal, and per-property
states in which any write to a constant property, of the same value too, makes it not constant;
define and delete covered; no hook in [[SetPrototypeOf]], since an own property of
String.prototype shadows everything above it and a primitive owns only indices and length.
Tests for every kind of write (assignment of the same and of another value, defineProperty as
data, accessor and attributes only, delete, a polyfill replacing one method while the others stay
fused, a property made non-writable, another Realm's String.prototype independent). Fork 2: the
fusion in the JIT at GetMethod + argument + CallWithThis(1) when the call IC holds the intrinsic,
a failed guard running the unfused templates. Fork 3: the region's register operands and facts.
Steps 1-4 as proposed, each measured before the next (counts, code bytes, Djot's elapsed time
against node-sp under the hold, TRust's three pages and the spike).

On main e3322606 (A2 landed) with Djot step 1 measured on its own binary (d2620672, on ea6fd916);
TRust JS citations at e3322606 (worktree target/p2/djot-gap/c4-wt).

THE LOOPS

Djot's block parser scans its subject with two methods (benchmarks/fixtures/djot.js, the bundle's
offsets 17658 and 17795):

  skipSpace(){const t=this.subject;let e=this.pos;for(;32===(s=t.codePointAt(e))||9===s;)e++;
    var s;this.indent=e-this.startline,this.pos=e}
  getEol(){const t=this.subject;let e=this.pos;for(;10!==(s=t.codePointAt(e))&&13!==s;)e++;
    var s;this.starteol=e,13===t.codePointAt(e)&&10===t.codePointAt(e+1)?this.endeol=e+1:
    this.endeol=e}

getEol runs once a line and scans it to its end; skipSpace runs several times a line and usually
scans nothing.

SIZE

On step 1 (d2620672, fat LTO, instructions:u, pacing off; target/p2/djot-gap/c4):
- Djot's steady state (the 40-pass variant): getEol's chunk 10.70% of the instructions, skipSpace's
  0.73% (perf record with TRUST_JS_PERF_MAP=1; size/p40-s1-symbols.txt).
- getEol, copied verbatim with a function driver over 1,000 lines, 200 and 400 times
  (micro/f-geteol-*): 227 instructions a character (226.5 over 20-character lines, 228.4 over 80),
  and 1,443 a call for an empty line, the driver's loop included.
- skipSpace, the same way (micro/f-skip-*): 976 instructions a call with no space to skip, of
  them 754 above the driver's loop, and 218 more for each space. By SPE, a call without a space
  spends about 365 instructions in skipSpace's own chunk (one evaluation of the loop's condition,
  this.subject and this.pos, the two stores) and the rest in the call and return, the caller's
  template and the shared stubs (candidate 5's).

Where a character's instructions go (SPE, one operation in 1,024, getEol's second-stage chunk on
the 80-character micro; dump/geteol2-spe-hot.txt). The loop is one register region; 95% of the
samples are in the chunk, about 194 instructions an iteration:

| part (the region's marks) | instructions an iteration |
| --- | ---: |
| GetMethod "codePointAt" (attributed to the LoadLocal before it) | 45.6 |
| the call template: callee identity, intrinsic dispatch, string and Number guards, the code point read | 57.0 |
| the region's glue around the call (the index's push, the result's classification) | 16.5 |
| the two StrictNotEq | 44.5 |
| JumpIfFalse and JumpIfFalsePeek | 19.5 |
| the back edge (Jump) | 4.9 |
| e++ (UpdateLocal), Pop, helper marks | 5.3 |

What one character pays for (the hot listing):
- GetMethod: the receiver's tag decoded (about 15 instructions of compares), ctx.interp and the
  active Realm's String.prototype loaded, its kind byte, its IC_PLAIN flag and its shape compared
  with the site's, the slot's bounds and its word loaded, the method pushed.
- The call: the callee word untagged and compared with the call IC's, the IC's epoch against
  the live one, the intrinsic's id dispatched, the receiver's String tag and the index's Number
  checked again, then the code point template (an exact index, the length, the buffer's form: the
  micro's subject is a view of a flat buffer).
- t and e live in registers (d9, d8), but the templates take their operands on the operand stack:
  each iteration stores t and e there and reads them back.
- Each StrictNotEq tests the tags of a code point the code just produced as a Number.

TRUST JS NOW

- The method read: jit.rs emit_prop_load_inline, with emit_packed_probe_receiver (a primitive's
  wrapper prototype from the active Realm, through ctx.interp: emit_load_active_proto). The
  probe's facts are the site cache's (IcState: shape, depth, slot), checked at each read.
- An assignment to String.prototype.codePointAt keeps the prototype's shape: the probe reloads the
  slot every time, and the call IC compares the callee with the one it recorded.
- The call: the call IC proves the callee is the codePointAt native, and the intrinsic dispatch
  runs emit_code_point_template (jit.rs, W3's item 2c).
- Writes to String.prototype already reach Rust: a String wrapper is kind 23, past
  KIND_ORDINARY_LAST (19; value.rs:2314, 2352), and the JIT's named stores admit ordinary kinds
  only (guard_exotic_ordinary in the store stub, jit.rs:13185-13187, and in the inline store,
  13344).
- Infrastructure to build on:
  - shapes, with FLAG_IC_PLAIN and FLAG_PROTO (a marked prototype);
  - PROTO_EPOCH (value.rs), bumped by structural changes of marked prototypes, for the creation
    caches;
  - CALL_IC_EPOCH for the call caches;
  - the dependency registry (dependency.rs, W4 step 10): JSC-style watchpoint sets, the first one
    a prototype's shape (Props::note_structural fires it). Its consumer is the speculative tier,
    which baseline chunks are not: a chunk has no invalidation point to leave at once.

WHAT THE EXEMPLARS DO

Current source: V8 41b0e42f (2026-11-05), SpiderMonkey (firefox) fa1e90ea (2026-11-05), WebKit
ab234b60 (2026-11-06); the files in target/p2/djot-gap/c4-src and exemplar-src. None has a
protector for String.prototype's methods as such. Each baseline guards the method's read at every
access, and each optimizing tier makes the method a constant through dependencies.

V8 (src/ paths):
- Sparkplug's named load calls a LoadIC builtin; Sparkplug+ (shipped) patches a site to a builtin
  for its handler, but a string receiver's site becomes LoadICGenericBaseline: the handler of a
  primitive receiver carries DoAccessCheckOnLookupStartObject (ic/handler-configuration.cc:41-62;
  objects/feedback-vector.cc:925-943; ic/ic.cc:856-873, 1015-1019).
- The feedback map is the string's own (every string map unstable), the holder String.prototype,
  the handler LoadFromPrototype with the method as a weak constant and String.prototype's
  prototype validity cell (ic/ic.cc:1422-1447; ic/handler-configuration.cc:119-149;
  objects/map.cc:2574-2639).
- Each access: the map compared, the cell loaded and compared with cleared, the cell's native
  context compared with the current one, the constant dereferenced (ic/accessor-assembler.cc:
  86-97, 1284-1293, 1309-1343, 1410-1443).
- The cell is invalidated lazily (its value set to cleared, objects/js-objects.cc:5398-5406) at
  any map change of String.prototype or a prototype above it (js-objects.cc:3302-3306,
  5436-5470), and when an assignment turns the method's const field mutable
  (objects/map-updater.cc:1272-1273).
- The call goes through a call builtin to the codePointAt builtin (Torque,
  builtins/builtins-string.tq:192-207): no in-line read in Sparkplug.
- TurboFan and Maglev: stable-map and field-constness dependencies fold the load to a constant
  (compiler/compilation-dependencies.cc:1548-1570, compiler/access-info.cc:763-768) and inline
  codePointAt (compiler/js-call-reducer.cc:7720-7750; maglev/maglev-reducer-inl.h:6868-6915).
- V8's protectors cover String's @@iterator, @@replace/@@split/@@matchAll, length overflow and
  ToPrimitive (execution/protectors.h:49-103), no method.

SpiderMonkey (js/src paths):
- The GetProp IC for a string (jit/CacheIR.cpp tryAttachPrimitive, 2647-2714): a tag test
  (GuardNonDoubleType), String.prototype as a stub constant, then, in its Specialized mode and
  with String.prototype's ObjectFuse, GuardObjectFuseProperty and the method returned as the
  stub's constant (2278-2295, 2341-2384). The fallback is a shape guard on String.prototype and
  the slot's load (2405, 914).
- The fuse check in the Baseline stub: the fuse's word "no constant property invalidated" loaded
  and compared with 0; otherwise its generation and the property's state bits
  (jit/CacheIRCompiler.cpp:11880-11957).
- The call IC (tryAttachStringChar, CacheIR.cpp:8275-8369): the callee's identity
  (GuardSpecificFunction), a string this, an Int32 index, then LoadStringCodePointResult in line
  in the stub (CacheIRCompiler.cpp:4926-4975; MacroAssembler.cpp:1769-1863). The native is never
  called.
- The ObjectFuse (vm/ObjectFuse.cpp): built-in prototypes have one (vm/GlobalObject.cpp:436-444).
  Watchtower hooks see assignments (vm/NativeObject.cpp:2486), defineProperty (1455), delete
  (vm/Shape.cpp:872) and prototype changes (1153). A write to a Constant property, even of the
  same value, marks it NotConstant, sets invalidatedConstantProperty and invalidates the dependent
  Ion code (ObjectFuse.cpp:114-137); structural changes bump the generation (139-175). Store ICs
  optimize only NotConstant properties (the note at ObjectFuse.cpp:121-123).
- Warp: the fuse a compile dependency, the method a constant, codePointAt inlined as MCodePointAt
  (jit/WarpCacheIRTranspiler.cpp:516-522, 1776-1781, 2806-2830).

JavaScriptCore (Source/JavaScriptCore paths):
- Baseline get_by_id (jit/JITPropertyAccess.cpp:548-583; jit/JITInlineCacheGenerator.cpp:
  162-168): the base's structure ID compared (one string structure a VM, runtime/VM.cpp:344),
  then the holder and offset from the IC and the slot loaded.
- StringPrototype's condition (Presence of codePointAt) is a watchpoint on its structure, adaptive
  (re-armed while the property is present), which resets the IC when it fires
  (bytecode/InlineCacheCompiler.cpp:3135-3143; bytecode/PropertyCondition.cpp:109-127, 366-369;
  bytecode/PropertyInlineCacheClearingWatchpoint.cpp:61-79). An assignment keeps the structure:
  the IC loads the new value and the call IC misses on the callee's identity.
- The call: a call IC (the callee's identity) to a codePointAt thunk: a String this that is no
  rope, an Int32 index in bounds, the unit, surrogates (jit/ThunkGenerators.cpp:893-934).
- DFG and FTL: the Presence promoted to a watched Equivalence, the method a constant, the
  StringCodePointAt node in line (dfg/DFGByteCodeParser.cpp:3780-3796, 7175-7177).
- JSGlobalObject's stringPrototypeChainIsSane set is about indexed properties
  (runtime/JSGlobalObject.cpp:3340-3342), not methods.

| engine | baseline: the method's read | baseline: the call | what invalidates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V8 | a builtin call: the string's map, String.prototype's validity cell and native context, the constant | builtins: feedback, the codePointAt builtin | the cell, lazily: a map change of String.prototype or above, a const field made mutable |
| SpiderMonkey | an IC stub: the tag, String.prototype's fuse word, the constant | an IC stub: the callee's identity, the tags, the code point in line | Watchtower: any write to a constant property, define, delete, a prototype change |
| JSC | the IC: the string structure, the slot | a call IC to a code point thunk | structure watchpoints; an assignment shows at the call IC |
| TRust JS now | in line: the tag decoded, the Realm's String.prototype, its kind, flag and shape, the slot | in line: the callee's identity and epoch, the intrinsic dispatch, the tags, the code point | the shape (structural changes); the identity (assignments) |

TRUST JS AGAINST THEM

- TRust JS's read checks String.prototype's own state at each access, which none of the three
  does: they hold it by a cell (V8), a fuse word (SpiderMonkey) or watchpoints (JSC).
- Its call already reads the code point in line, as SpiderMonkey's Baseline does; JSC calls a
  thunk and V8 a builtin.
- The cost is in the read's checks (45.6 instructions) and in the call's identity check, epoch,
  dispatch and repeated tag tests (57.0), and in the operand stack between ops whose values the
  region holds in registers.

THE FORKS

Fork 1, the guard on the method:
- (a) SpiderMonkey's ObjectFuse: String.prototype gets a fuse, a word that stays 0 while none of
  its tracked properties (its built-in methods) has been written, and a state per property. Every
  write to String.prototype (assignment, defineProperty, delete) goes through Rust already; the
  hook there marks the property and sets the word. A site checks the tag and the word (one load
  from the active Realm, one compare), and then knows the method is the one it implements.
  - Only String.prototype's own property matters. A primitive string's own properties are its
    indices and length, so a method name is never one of them, and String.prototype's
    [[SetPrototypeOf]] cannot change what its own property holds.
  - As now, the active Realm's String.prototype is the one read: the code point is the same
    whichever Realm's codePointAt runs it, and only the slow paths can throw.
- (b) V8's validity cell: a cell per prototype's shape, cleared at any shape change and when an
  assignment changes a constant field's constness. TRust's shapes are ids without cells, and its
  fields have no constness.
- (c) JSC's watchpoints: the dependency registry has the sets, but a baseline chunk cannot leave
  at once when one fires (no invalidation points), so a site would still check something, and an
  assignment keeps the shape: the read would still load the slot, and the call compare identity.
- (d) Keep today's re-validation and only trim it (the tag decode, the shape check).

Recommendation: (a), SpiderMonkey's. It is the one exemplar baseline that does this exact case
in one word, and its invalidation fits where TRust's writes to String.prototype already go. Two
levels, as SpiderMonkey's: the word for the fast path, and the property's own state when the word
is set, so that a polyfill replacing one method keeps the others fast.

Decided (the coordinator's, 2026-11-07): all three forks as recommended. Fork 1 matches
SpiderMonkey's semantics (vm/ObjectFuse.h's SMDOC and ObjectFuse.cpp; vm/Watchtower.cpp;
vm/NativeObject.cpp at fa1e90ea), not a simplification of them:
- State per property (two bits): Untracked, Constant (generated code may rely on it), NotConstant
  (written after it was Constant). Marking a property Constant is the JIT's, as SpiderMonkey's
  tryOptimizeConstantProperty (ObjectFuse.cpp:91-110): Untracked becomes Constant, NotConstant
  stays refused.
- A value change (ObjectFuse::handlePropertyValueChange, ObjectFuse.cpp:114-137; called before
  the same-value check, Watchtower.cpp:755-764): Untracked becomes Constant, Constant becomes
  NotConstant and sets the word, NotConstant stays. It is every write of the value, the same
  value included, and every defineProperty that is not redundant: SpiderMonkey's define of a data
  property calls it after changing the flags (NativeObject.cpp:1449-1457), so a define that only
  makes the method non-writable counts too. A redundant define changes nothing
  (DefinePropertyIsRedundant, NativeObject.cpp:1569-1626, 1741-1747). An accessor in place of the
  method, or a new getter, is a value change.
- Freezing and sealing change flags only (NativeObject::freezeOrSealProperties, Shape.cpp:
  1031-1060; Watchtower's watchPropertyFlagsChange and watchFreezeOrSeal leave the fuse alone,
  Watchtower.cpp:703-735, 829-847): String.prototype frozen keeps its methods fused, as a hardened
  (SES) environment's intrinsics need.
- Removing a tracked property bumps the generation and sets the word
  (ObjectFuse::handlePropertyRemove, ObjectFuse.cpp:139-160). TRust's maps close the gap a removal
  leaves (Props::remove_key), so the states after it move down with their properties; the bumped
  generation fails every guard that named a slot.
- The other generation bumps SpiderMonkey lists (shape teleporting's shadowing and proto
  mutation, the global lexical environment, object swapping) do not apply: TRust has no shape
  teleporting, and the fuse's object is String.prototype.
- No [[SetPrototypeOf]] hook. A primitive string's own properties are its indices and length
  (String exotic objects' [[GetOwnProperty]], ECMA-262 StringGetOwnProperty), so a method's name
  is never one of them, and the lookup's first hop is String.prototype. String.prototype's own
  property shadows everything above it; changing String.prototype's [[Prototype]] cannot change
  what that own property holds. Removing it is a removal, which the fuse sees.
- The site's guard (SpiderMonkey's GuardObjectFuseProperty, jit/CacheIRCompiler.cpp:11880-11957):
  the word is 0, or the generation is the one recorded when the site was compiled and the
  property's NotConstant bit is clear.

Fork 2, where the fused step is chosen:
- (a) In the JIT, at GetMethod "codePointAt" followed by its argument and CallWithThis(1), when
  the call IC holds the codePointAt intrinsic (in a first stage, by the name, still guarded). A
  failed guard runs the unfused templates. This is what SpiderMonkey's IC stubs do for
  primitive receivers; JSC's thunk and V8's optimizing tiers choose at the call too.
- (b) A bytecode op from the compiler: it cannot know the receiver is a string.

Recommendation: (a).

Fork 3, the loop's values in registers: no exemplar baseline does it (their optimizing tiers
do). In the region, the fused step reads t and e from their registers, leaves s in one with a
Number fact (a code point, or undefined past the end, which keeps the boxed form), and the two
StrictNotEq against constants compare it without tag tests and branch on the flags. This is the
plan's second half.

PLAN

1. The fuse. A word per Realm next to string_proto in InterpLayout, with a state per tracked
   property (String.prototype's built-in methods). The hooks: the Rust paths that write, define
   or delete a property of a Realm's String.prototype; any define of a tracked property counts as
   a write, attributes alone included. Tests, in every tier: each kind of write, a write of the
   same value, a getter in place of the method, freezing, another Realm's String.prototype, an
   unrelated method replaced (the others stay fast), a String object and other primitives as
   receivers.
2. ARM64 templates: the fused step for codePointAt. The guards: a primitive string receiver, the
   site's fuse being the active Realm's, the fuse's word (then the property's state), a Number
   index; the code point template as now; any miss takes the existing sequence. Then charCodeAt
   and charAt, which tokenizers use (Web Tooling's acorn, esprima and the others).
   - A site's data (chunk-owned, as a call cache's way): the fuse it was validated in and its
     guard data. A chunk runs in whichever Realm is active, and the probe reads the active Realm's
     prototype, so the step compares the active Realm's fuse with the site's.
   - The fill, in the slow path: the active Realm's String.prototype holds its own codePointAt
     as a data property, and that value is the Realm's built-in; then try_optimize_constant. The
     value must be checked as the site fills: a property replaced while Untracked becomes
     Constant with the new value (SpiderMonkey's handlePropertyValueChange), and a SpiderMonkey
     stub returns the value it recorded, where this step runs the built-in's algorithm.
3. The region: the fused step on register operands, and the Number fact for its result.
4. x86-64 runs GetMethod through its helper (jit_x64.rs:1265) and has no in-line read: there the
   fused guard would skip that helper and the call's and call the intrinsic's. A later step.

EXPECTED SIZE

From the SPE breakdown, a character in getEol would go from about 194 instructions to about 45:
- the read, the call and their glue, 119, to about 25: the tag, the word, the index, the read;
- the two StrictNotEq, 44.5, to about 6;
- the branches, 19.5, to about 4;
- the back edge and e++, about 7, unchanged.

getEol is 10.70% of the steady state's instructions, so that would be about 8% of them. skipSpace
would lose about 150 of its 750 instructions a call; its call and return are candidate 5's.
Elapsed time: measured per step; Djot needs about 5% more to reach 77 ms.

### Djot's candidate 4, steps 1 and 2: String.prototype's fuse, codePointAt and charCodeAt fused (record, 2026-11-07)

Landed by fast-forward on main 87a05b21 (an agent's): 29a5dbac (String.prototype's ObjectFuse:
which of its methods generated code may treat as constant), 46229f9b (step 2a: GetMethod
"codePointAt", its index and CallWithThis(1) as one step in the ARM64 templates, in line in loops
and through a process-wide shared stub elsewhere), 4abc8062 (step 2b: charCodeAt too; the code
unit, NaN past the end, for any string form). The agent's working note, with the details below,
is target/p2/djot-gap/c4/design-note.txt.

Two bugs found in step 1 while step 2 was written, latent while nothing read the fuse, fixed in
29a5dbac with tests:
- Interp::swap_realm (an embedder's Realm entry and exit, with_realm_snapshot) swapped
  string_proto but not its fuse: a site could have checked another Realm's fuse. The fuse and its
  address now swap together (every_realm_switch_carries_the_string_prototypes_fuse).
- A property's removal moves the later slots down in TRust, where SpiderMonkey's slots stay put:
  removing an untracked property before a constant one moved the constant's slot without a new
  generation, and remove_key skipped the hook for index keys among the named entries, so a site's
  (index, mask) could name the wrong state bits. handle_remove now bumps the generation whenever a
  tracked state sits at or after the removed slot, and remove_key reports every removal (tests: an
  earlier property's removal, an index key's).

A site's data is its chunk's (the fuse's address, generation, index, mask, and a Weak pin so that
no later fuse takes the address); the fill runs in the slow path (H_STRING_CALL_FILL), and a
refused site stores the address with bit 0 set and stops asking until a new generation. The step is
chosen when the call cache holds the native or nothing (the VM fills no native call-cache
entries; a fused first stage leaves the cache empty for the second stage). charAt waits for a path
from generated code to the single-unit strings (V8's single_character_string_table through its
roots, SpiderMonkey's StaticStrings, JSC's vm.smallStrings; in TRust through ctx.interp).

Measured (the series head against main 87a05b21; fat LTO; the agent's checks/):
- instructions: Djot -0.13%, Crypto -0.22%, TypeScript +0.19%, RegExp +0.08%, DeltaBlue +0.05%, the
  rest within +-0.04%. TypeScript's is layout: on one binary the fused calls save it 0.19% and
  Crypto 0.24% (a switch, environments of equal length), and that binary with them off counts
  +0.15% against main.
- code: Vue 425,552 (-8), React unchanged, Djot 2,450,304 (+5,792).
- Djot's elapsed time (the hold, CPU 5, 10 rounds, medians): main 79 ms, the series 78 ms,
  node-sp 38.5 ms. Djot's loops run in register regions, which these steps' templates do not
  reach: step 3 carries the loops' gain.

Checks: the gate on b4389c75 (the head's code but for cfg(test) attributes of five test-only
functions and a test helper removed; the fat-LTO .text identical): rustfmt; the lib suite 2,881
passed, with pacing on 2,881; the fixtures as the base; difftest 138 agree; Test262 53,575/53,575,

### Djot's gap, candidate 3: RegExp exec's runtime, measured piece by piece (census and forks, 2026-11-07)

On main 63eb71df (fat LTO, target/p2/lto/63eb71df, identical to 4abc8062's binary), instructions:u
at CPU 14 with TRUST_JS_GC_PACING=0; micro-benchmarks in target/p2/djot-gap/c3/micro, Djot's own
profiles in c3/census. Exemplar sources (target/p2/djot-gap/c3/src, data only; PINS.txt), each file
fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at its pin: V8 main 41b0e42f (2026-11-05, the W6 pin; c3/src/v8),
SpiderMonkey firefox fa1e90ea, WebKit ab234b60.

THE CALLS

Djot's exec calls (27,246 a run, TRUST_JS_JIT_NATIVESTAT=1) are of two kinds (TRUST_JS_REGEXP_PROF=2,
census/djot-prof2.err):

| kind | executions a run | matched | result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `find`'s patterns, `new RegExp(src, "yd")` | 16,610 | 4,092 (3,652 without captures) | null, or an array with `indices` |
| the inline parser's specials scan, `/[\r\n"'()*+.:<=[\\\]^_\`${}~-]/g`, and two more /g | about 10,600 | nearly all | an array of one unit, no captures |

find (benchmarks/fixtures/djot.js, module 481):

  find(t, e, s, n) { e.lastIndex = s; i = n !== undefined ? t.substring(0, n + 1) : t;
    const r = e.exec(i); if (r !== null) { const t = []; if (r.indices.length > 1)
    for (let e = 1; e < r.indices.length; e++) { const [s, n] = r.indices[e];
    t.push(i.substring(s, n)) } return { startpos: r.indices[0][0], endpos: r.indices[0][1] - 1,
    captures: t } } return null }

The specials pattern runs on two-byte subjects (all 10,472 of its executions) through the
matcher's single-element path in Rust (Regex::find_single, next_start::<&[u16]>), not native code.

THE PIECES

Each variant runs one sticky pattern in a loop of 100,000 and 300,000 iterations over a subject
it matches at every third unit; the regexps and the subject are arguments (micro/pieces2.js), and
the difference of the two counts over 200,000 prices an iteration:

| variant | instructions an iteration | the piece it adds |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| v0: the loop | 95 | |
| v1: `re.lastIndex = pos` | 168 | the lastIndex store, 73 |
| v2: `re.exec(subject)` missing | 1,104 | an exec that fails, 936 |
| v3: `re.exec(subject).index` matching | 2,167 | a match's result, 1,063 more |
| v4: with `d` and two captures, `r.indices[1][1] - r.indices[1][0]` | 4,420 | two captures, the indices and their reads, 2,253 more |
| v5: v4 destructuring `const [s, e] = r.indices[1]` | 4,652 | destructuring a pair, 232 more |
| v6: `re.test(subject)` matching | 1,578 | |

Where an exec goes (perf record, instructions:u at 100,000, TRUST_JS_PERF_MAP and TRUST_JS_JIT_MAP;
instructions an iteration):

| | miss (v2) | match (v3) | match, `d`, 2 captures (v4) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| the native call: jit_call_hit, call_native_committed_with (with its two interrupt polls, RuntimeInterrupt::current_reason out of line), with_borrowed_values, activate_agent | 272 | 300 | 303 |
| the call's templates (GetMethod, CallWithThis, the call stubs) | about 190 | about 110 | about 110 |
| regexp_exec and regexp_builtin_exec (arguments, flags, lastIndex's handling) | 146 | 317 | 436 |
| lastIndex read at its slot (slot_last_index) | 42 | 50 | 55 |
| the matcher's entry: regexp_exec_text_shared (exec_at, exec_impl_with, native::run's setup) | 45 | 140 | 137 |
| the match itself (the native program, regex::native::run) | small | 80 | 139 |
| Captures::from_slots | | 94 | 108 |
| the legacy statics (update_regexp_legacy_statics, realm_regexp_constructor) | | 138 | 112 |
| the match array (regexp_array, alloc_empty, alloc_block, the match string) | | 430 | |
| the indices and the captures (pair arrays: alloc_empty, alloc_block, init_packed_array, array_length_shape and _layout; capture strings: unit_lstr, alloc_string_cell) | | | about 1,900 |
| reading the result (`.index`, `.indices`, element reads) | | about 110 | about 450 |

A correction to the first draft: the interrupt polls are the native call's, not the matcher's.
call_native_committed_with polls RuntimeInterrupt::current_reason before and after every native
(interpreter.rs:16314, :16327), about 16 instructions each; the matcher polls only on long scans
(regex.rs:2202, :2480). They belong to candidate 2's boundary.

In Djot's steady state (the 40-pass variant from its start, instructions:u at 20,000,
census/djot-p40-ins.txt): exec's runtime in Rust is 2.93% of the instructions (regexp_builtin_exec
0.84%, regexp_exec 0.46%, regexp_exec_text_shared 0.43%, regexp_array 0.30%, slot_last_index 0.27%,
the statics 0.27%, from_slots 0.16%, the rest 0.20%), its allocations a share of alloc_empty's
1.01% and alloc_string_cell's 0.85%; the matching 1.91%, of which the specials scan's
single-element path on two-byte subjects is about 0.9% (next_start::<&[u16]> 0.47%, find_single
0.19%, first_matches 0.12%, CharClass::matches_raw2 0.11%) and the native programs under 0.4%.
In cycles (the census) exec's runtime around the match was 5.3-5.9%: allocation-heavy code runs
more cycles an instruction.

Sized by kind, a run's exec runtime in instructions (the call excluded): find's misses about
12,500 x 500, find's matches about 3,650 x 1,800 (one pair) and 440 x 3,400 (captures), the
specials' matches about 10,600 x 1,200.

THE EXEMPLARS, PIECE BY PIECE

- The entry. V8: RegExpPrototypeExec is a JS builtin the call IC enters with no C++ transition
  (src/builtins/regexp-exec.tq:31-43); its fast path is one map compare against the RegExp
  function's initial map and a positive-Smi lastIndex (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:1166-1191,
  IsFastRegExpNoPrototype). SpiderMonkey: exec is self-hosted and its matcher is a JIT stub
  (jit/CodeGenerator.cpp:2953-3290, GenerateRegExpMatchStubShared). JSC: exec is C++
  (runtime/RegExpObjectInlines.h:214-250, RegExpObject::execInline) reached through the host
  function thunk.
- lastIndex. V8 loads and stores the in-object field (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:149-168,
  FastLoadLastIndexBeforeSmiCheck, FastStoreLastIndex; regexp.tq:339-366). JSC keeps it in the
  RegExpObject and reads it as a UInt32 (RegExpObjectInlines.h:188-206). SpiderMonkey's stub
  loads it from the RegExpObject's slot (CodeGenerator.cpp:3013, loadRegExpLastIndex).
- The match registers. V8 matches into a per-isolate static offsets vector, taken and returned
  around each exec (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:536-618, LoadOrAllocateRegExpResultVector and
  FreeRegExpResultVector), and copies
  it into the native context's RegExpMatchInfo (:653-692). SpiderMonkey's stub keeps the
  MatchPairs in its caller's frame (CodeGenerator.cpp:2364-2405). JSC matches into the RegExp's
  own ovector (RegExpMatchesArray.h:112, ovectorSpan).
- The legacy statics. V8: the RegExpMatchInfo in the running native context is the record; each
  match writes its subject and registers there (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:621-692,
  PrepareMatchInfo, InitializeMatchInfoFromRegisters), and the statics' strings are made when
  read. SpiderMonkey: the C++ path copies the pairs (builtin/RegExp.cpp:349-368;
  vm/RegExpStatics.h:288-296, updateFromMatchPairs); the JIT stub records lazily, the source,
  flags, input and lastIndex with pendingLazyEvaluation, skipping the pointer stores when the
  source and input are unchanged (CodeGenerator.cpp:2265-2349, UpdateRegExpStatics), and a read
  re-executes (RegExpStatics.h:21-43, executeLazy). JSC: recordMatch stores the regexp, the input
  and the match's start and end in the global object's RegExpGlobalData
  (runtime/RegExpGlobalDataInlines.h:92-96; RegExpObjectInlines.h:248), and a read re-runs the
  match (RegExpCachedResult.h:42-79, RegExpCachedResult.cpp:49, lastResult). All three find the
  record from the running realm (V8's native context slot, SpiderMonkey's global, JSC's global
  object) without looking up the constructor.
- The match array. V8 allocates it uninitialized from the native context's result map, the
  elements with it (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:56-145, AllocateRegExpResult,
  AllocateUninitializedJSArrayWithElements), index, input and groups in-object, then stores
  SubStrings (:323-380). SpiderMonkey: one dense array of the realm's cached match-result shape,
  fully allocated, elements initialized in place as dependent strings (builtin/RegExp.cpp:92-148,
  NewDenseFullyAllocatedArrayWithShape). JSC: an uninitialized butterfly and cell of the global
  object's matches-array structure, out-of-line properties written directly
  (RegExpMatchesArray.h:59-106).
- The indices. V8: a runtime call after the result (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:500-505,
  Runtime_RegExpBuildIndices, runtime-regexp.cc:1037-1048), which allocates a FixedArray(2) and a
  JSArray for each pair (src/objects/js-regexp.cc:20-58). SpiderMonkey: an array of a cached
  indices shape, each pair NewDenseFullyAllocatedArray(cx, 2) initialized in place
  (builtin/RegExp.cpp:150-200); its JIT stub does not build indices or groups at all and goes
  out of line for them (CodeGenerator.cpp:3025-3036). JSC: the indices array of its structure,
  each pair through tryConstructArrayPair, under one GCDeferralContext
  (RegExpMatchesArray.cpp:92-200).

WHAT TRUST DOES THAT THEY DO NOT

1. The statics: each match finds the running Realm's %RegExp% through the RegExp protector's
   pins (regexp::realm_regexp_constructor: a RefCell borrow, the pins, a Weak upgrade), compares
   it with the record's, and copies the spans into Interp::regexp_last's Vec: 112-138 a match.
   The record could be keyed by the running Realm as the exemplars key it (the global object,
   which swap_realm exchanges, is at hand) and resolve the constructor when an accessor reads it.
2. The spans travel three times: the native slots into the scratch's caps (native::run), the
   caps into a Captures (from_slots, 94-108), the Captures into the statics' Vec; V8 copies its
   registers once (into the match info) and builds the result from there, JSC builds from the
   ovector directly.
3. lastIndex: slot_last_index reads the protector's instance shape under a RefCell borrow and an
   environment flag, borrows the object, compares its shape, and tests the slot's Number for
   writable, finite, non-negative and integral (42-55); regexp_program clones the matcher's Rc
   (regexp_exec). V8's fast path is a map compare and a Smi test.
4. The result's arrays go through the generic object path: a cell (alloc_empty) and an element
   block (alloc_block) each, and for a pair the array `length` shape and layout looked up again
   (array_length_shape, array_length_layout: two thread-local heap lookups, a RefCell borrow and
   an Rc clone). The match arrays already share a template map (regexp_array_maps); the pairs and
   the result's cell do not. The exemplars allocate each from a fixed map, shape or structure in
   one or two bump allocations and fill it in place.
5. The call: the native call boundary (about 270 with its two interrupt polls) and the call
   templates (110-190) are candidate 2's (a native's fast entry from generated code); exec is its
   biggest client.
6. The specials scan: a single-element program over a two-byte subject scans in Rust
   (find_single, next_start::<&[u16]>, about 0.9% of Djot's instructions). V8 tiers every
   pattern up from its bytecode to irregexp's native code (src/regexp/regexp.cc:842-862), whose
   scan for a class is machine code; TRust's single-element path never takes native code.

THE FORKS (for the coordinator, with a recommendation each)

Fork 1. Where exec's fast path runs.
  (a) In Rust, entered through candidate 2's native fast entry: JSC's model (execInline, C++,
      through the host function thunk), with the pieces below cut in Rust.
  (b) In generated code: a stub that reads lastIndex, runs the native program and builds the
      result (SpiderMonkey's RegExpMatcher stub; V8's CSA builtin).
  Recommendation: (a). Djot's `find` patterns all carry `d`: SpiderMonkey's stub goes out of
  line for exactly these (CodeGenerator.cpp:3025-3036) and V8 builds their indices in C++ through
  a runtime call, so the exemplar of a stub does not stub this case. What the exemplars keep fast
  (lastIndex as a field, registers in a reused buffer, results from fixed shapes, the statics
  as a cheap record) Rust can do; what a stub adds beyond them is the call boundary, which
  candidate 2 removes for every native. (b) stays open for the specials-style /g exec without
  `d` once (a) is measured.

Fork 2. The legacy statics.
  (a) V8's: record the subject and the spans in the running Realm's record at every match.
  (b) SpiderMonkey's JIT path and JSC's: record the regexp, the subject and the search start (and
      the whole match), and recompute the captures when a static is read; SpiderMonkey skips the
      record's pointer stores when nothing changed.
  Recommendation: (b), the record keyed by the running Realm's global, the constructor found when
  an accessor reads. TRust already has (b)'s form (update_regexp_legacy_statics_lazy and
  flush_regexp_legacy's re-execution) for dead-result operations; (a) is V8's because its
  registers already sit in the match info that its result builder reads, and TRust's do not.

Fork 3. The result's arrays.
  (a) A pre-shaped image per kind (match, match with indices, indices, and the pair), kept per
      Agent beside regexp_array_maps: one cell and one element block each, the shape, layout and
      named slots written from the image (JSC's tryCreateUninitializedRegExpMatchesArray and
      tryConstructArrayPair, SpiderMonkey's cached shapes, V8's result maps).
  (b) Leave regexp_builtin_exec's arrays to the generic Object::new_built and make the generic
      allocation cheaper.
  Recommendation: (a), measured per kind. (b) is the allocator's own work across all objects,
  beyond this candidate; (a) is what all three do for these four kinds regardless of their
  allocators' speed.

Not forks (each the exemplars' only form): the spans copied once, from the matcher's slots
straight into the result and the record (2); lastIndex read as V8 and JSC read it, a shape
compare and the slot's word, and the matcher reached without cloning its Rc (3); the interrupt
polls left to the matcher's long scans and to candidate 2's boundary.

PLAN (each step measured against main on its own, counts, code bytes and timing as candidate 4's)

- Step 1: the statics by the running Realm, recorded lazily (fork 2), and the spans copied once:
  about 200-250 instructions a match.
- Step 2: lastIndex at its slot as V8 reads it, and the matcher without the Rc clone: about
  50-100 an exec, misses included.
- Step 3: the four array kinds from their images (fork 3): about 100 a pair and some of the match
  array's 430.
- Then, measured: the specials' single-element scan over two-byte subjects (6), and whether a
  stub for plain /g exec (fork 1's (b)) still pays once candidate 2's entry is in.

EXPECTED SIZE

Steps 1-3 cut about a third to a half of exec's runtime: of Djot's steady state, about 1.0-1.5% of
the instructions and, with the allocations' cycles, perhaps 1.5-2.5% of the time. The call
boundary (candidate 2) and the specials scan (about 0.9%) come on top.

DECIDED (the coordinator, 2026-11-07, under the owner's standing approval): forks 1(a), 2(b) and
3(a); fork 1(b), a stub for plain /g exec without `d`, stays open until (a) and candidate 2's entry
are measured. Conditions: the lazy record holds what re-execution needs in immutable form (the
compiled program, not the RegExp object, which Annex B's compile() re-points; tested); the
per-Realm record travels with every Realm switch (tested like the string fuse's); today's
legacy-statics behaviour is kept (every match updates the running Realm's record, as V8, JSC and
SpiderMonkey's default builds do: TRust has no [[LegacyFeaturesEnabled]], and Test262's 24
legacy-regexp tests check only the accessors' receivers); the record is traced; the images (step
3) follow the running Realm's %Array.prototype%, fill in place with every slot GC-safe before the
next allocation, and keep W6's allocation-colour and barrier rule; steps 1 and 3 are checked with
Test262 under GC stress and under TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=force and a churn repro that holds
results across many execs.

STEP 4, THE MATCH-ARRAY IMAGE: SIZED, NOT TAKEN (the coordinator, 2026-11-07)

Where a match array's ~200 instructions go (step 1's exec-against-test() profile on the sticky
micro, an array a match):

| piece | instructions | an image avoids |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| regexp_array, init_array_from_template, extend_fresh | about 67 | most of it |
| alloc_empty (the cell, through the page's free bitmap, about 30 of it) | 40-70 | the struct building only |
| alloc_block (the separate element block) | 53-65 | none |

An image of the whole body (fork 3(a)'s form, memcpy and patch) removes the generic map's
defaults, the template's checks, extend_fresh's branch and the Object built on the stack and moved:
about 50 a match array, about 0.7M of Djot's instructions a run (-0.14%). The exemplars' cheapness
is mostly the allocation: V8's AllocateUninitializedJSArrayWithElements allocates the JSArray and
its FixedArray as one bump allocation (builtins-regexp-gen.cc:56-145), SpiderMonkey's
NewDenseFullyAllocatedArrayWithShape keeps the elements in the object (fixed elements), both from
nursery bump allocation. One allocation for a small array's cell and its elements would save about
110 a match array, and every small array literal, split and match result with it: an object-model
change to DenseStorage/Words (a block inside its cell, moved out on growth), carried to the owner as
a P3 item. An image on today's two allocations would be rewritten by it: throwaway unsafe code for
-0.14% of Djot. Candidate 3 is steps 1 and 3.

THE PROPERTY-STUB CENSUS (the coordinator's (3); no proposal)

SPE branch samples (branch_filter=1, -c 256) of djot-p40 from 400 ms, CPU 13, on ac414fd3; a branch
from a chunk into a Stub:Prop* range is a stub entry, its call site mapped by TRUST_JS_JIT_MAP
(props/propstub-report.txt, propstub-report.py). Of 1,556 sampled entries, PropRead 1,038 (67%),
PropWays, the way-loop form for polymorphic sites, 330 (21%), PropWrite 188 (12%). The sites are
many and flat (the largest 40 hold 12-58 samples each): `this.matches`, for-of's `value` and
`done`, `length` at four sites of next and others, `push`, `exec`, `.index`, the block parser's
`startline`, `pos` and `subject`, `lastIndex` writes, `renderAstNode`. They are the first-stage
named reads and writes outside loops (emit_prop_read_site, jit.rs:7455-7470), which V8's Sparkplug
makes as LoadIC_Baseline calls and SpiderMonkey's Baseline as its sites' shared IC stubs; a fifth
are polymorphic. No stub defect; about 5.3% of the steady state's cycles. Cheaper would mean baking
hot monomorphic non-loop sites in line: a second-stage or tier question, after candidate 2 and the
matcher entry.

### Candidate 2, step 1: a light native's fast entry from generated code (record, 2026-11-07)

The design note's (a) for the light classes ("### A native's fast entry from generated code;
includes, indexOf and substring in line", decided A1, B2, C1). Lands as ae0dee7f on main bfb58035,
the first of three commits (with step 2's 51308858 and the trims' dad9d67f); measured as dc40ded6
on main 63eb71df (fat LTO lto/main-63eb71df), the same patch but for its helper index (37 after
candidate 4's H_STRING_READ; the call-hit stub's key is 0x1500, after Stub:StringCall). Earlier
measurements of the same change: on main e3322606 as 9474fdd8 (p2-c2-native-e332), on 6725b6d6 as
37a23690 (p2-c2-native-w6) and on 87a05b21 as 28a9dfb6 (p2-c2-native-87); its A2 test fix landed
on its own as 10335559.

WHAT CHANGED

- A call site's call-hit form (its call-cache hit declined the direct sequence) calls a
  process-wide shared stub, SharedStub::CallHit, one for each arity up to eight and receiver form
  (jit::emit_call_hit_stub). The way records a stub kind (CallIc::native_stub, in padding at
  offset 97), chosen from the native's class when the way is filled (bytecode::native_stub_kind),
  as SpiderMonkey's call IC picks its native stub when it attaches: the class's operand test as
  bytecode::native_operands makes it (none: the operand-only collections' methods, the light
  class, Array.isArray, Object.is; every argument a Number: numeric-only and Math's; every
  argument a primitive: parseInt's class, isNaN, fromCharCode; the receiver and every argument
  primitives: String's primitive class and its templates' natives), and whether the class holds
  constructors (the light class: Boolean; the primitive-argument class: Number and String), whose
  natives read the construct state. The stub reads the kind (two instructions to the helper for
  anything else), makes the test in line and, for a constructor's class, checks that the caller
  is not constructing, then enters the native through one extern "C" fast entry,
  bytecode::jit_native_light, with no decode of the call. The native's errors record the call's
  position, which the site places two instructions past the return address. Anything else (a
  user callee, a native of no light class, DataView's and Reflect's natives, operands the test
  refuses, a constructing caller of a constructor's class) calls the call-hit helper as before.
  The fill asserts that no constructor is in a class the stub runs without its construct state.
- The site: `bl` to the stub, `cbz` to the join, `b` to the unwind, the position word: six words
  (compact code's helper form was five, the in-line form nine).
- No depth gate (the note's step 1 listed one): the light classes' natives run no author code,
  and the helper's light path (Interp::call_native_light) runs them on the caller's stack with no
  depth count or stack growth, as SpiderMonkey's, JSC's and V8's native entries do (a native that
  recurses checks its own stack). The gate belongs to step 2's boundary natives.
- TRUST_JS_JIT_NO_NATIVE_STUB=1 keeps the call-hit helper's call (DIAGNOSTICS.md).
- Tests (jit::native_stub_tests, 6).

THE NOISE. With incremental marking on (the default since 6725b6d6) one binary's counts move from
run to run: a slice's budget follows the wall clock (gc_core.rs slice_bytes: the cycle's elapsed
time against CYCLE_MARKING_TIME; SLICE_MAX_TIME's deadline; the preclean's deadline checks), so
the marking each slice does, the number of slices and the final pause's place move with timing.
Five runs of the step's binary (counts/c2s1-noise-28a9dfb6.txt): EarleyBoyer spread 8.0M (0.26%,
in two clusters), Splay 0.29M (0.025%, two clusters), PdfJS 0.10M; with TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=0
(against an equal-length dummy) 0.001% each. The medians of three can land in different clusters,
which is how the same toggle moved by about 0.2% between builds (on 6725b6d6: Splay +0.15%, PdfJS
-0.20%; here -0.01% and +0.02%). Apart from that, two binaries differ by more than the stub in
two workloads, with marking off too (counts/c2s1-incoff-28a9dfb6.txt, three runs each, spread
0.001%): EarleyBoyer main 3,101.52M against the step's 3,081.59M (-0.64%) and RayTrace 987.98M
against 986.15M (-0.19%), where the stub itself, toggled on the step's binary with marking off,
is -0.02% (3,082.14M to 3,081.62M) and +0.01% (986.02M to 986.17M). The cause of that binary
difference is not established. For attributing a JIT change, counts with TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL
=0 repeat to 0.001%.

### Candidate 2, step 2: the lean boundary's fast entry, and Reflect's (record, 2026-11-07)

The design note's (a) for the natives that may run author code ("### A native's fast entry from
generated code; includes, indexOf and substring in line", decided A1, B2, C1; B2 revised below),
with Reflect.get, has and set's own kind (decided 2026-11-07). Lands as 51308858 on step 1's
ae0dee7f (main bfb58035) (691c6f30 before a test-only amendment: the deadline test arms its
deadline inside the loop); measured as cde9bc81 on dc40ded6 (main 63eb71df), the same patch but for
its helper indices (38-40).

WHAT CHANGED

- The call-hit stub enters every engine native without the call-hit helper's decode of the
  call. Two stub kinds join the light ones (bytecode::native_stub_kind, chosen at fill):
  Reflect.get, has and set (bytecode::jit_native_reflect: answered on the operands as the helper
  answers them, Interp::reflect_resolved, else through the lean boundary), and the boundary's
  (bytecode::jit_native_boundary), for every other native of no light class and for a light
  class's native whose operands the stub's test refuses. Reflect.apply (its operand-only path)
  and DataView's accessors (light for some operands) keep the helper, as do user callees and
  scoped natives. V8's ReflectGet and ReflectHas are Torque javascript builtins
  (src/builtins/reflect.tq, calling GetPropertyWithReceiver and HasProperty) that Baseline code
  enters without a C++ boundary.
- A light class that holds constructors, on a constructing caller (the stub's machine-code test of
  the construct state), enters through bytecode::jit_native_light_construct, which saves and
  clears the construct state around the native, as the helper's light path does, where step 1
  sent it to the helper: a constructing caller's Number, String and Boolean stay light. (A first
  form that moved the test into that entry for every call of those classes cost Number.isInteger
  and parseInt 11 and 12 instructions a call, e1209d0a, not kept.)
- The lean boundary, Interp::call_native_lean (B2 revised): it keeps the depth and its stack
  checkpoint (nested calls count; a deep recursion through natives reports its RangeError), the
  construct state, the Agent restore (with_host_callback), the pending tail a native leaves, and
  the interrupt poll after the native; it drops the poll before the native and the safepoint at
  its entry. The call-hit helper's boundary arm and the generic helper's fill take it on both
  architectures.
- Tests (jit::native_stub_tests, 12 now; jit::poll_tests, 2 new, ARM64: a loop of an allocating
  native's calls collects at its back edge; a deadline the loop arms through a test native after
  its third Object.keys call stops it, so a loaded machine cannot pass the deadline before the
  loop's first native call, as the coordinator found the first version could). Candidate 4's fused
  String calls (63eb71df) come ahead of the call: a codePointAt site whose fuse step misses (a
  String object receiver, a String index) runs the unfused templates and the call, whose native
  the stub enters through the lean boundary or the light entry
  (fused_string_sites_that_miss_their_fuse_take_the_stub).

B2 REVISED (decided 2026-11-07). The note's B2 dropped both interrupt polls, as V8, SpiderMonkey
and JSC poll in JavaScript code only. Their natives, though, carry a termination out themselves:
V8's as the isolate's termination exception, an uncatchable pending exception that CEntry's
check of the exception sentinel after every C++ builtin propagates; SpiderMonkey's as a false
return with no pending exception (uncatchable); JSC's as its TerminationException. TRust's
NativeFn returns Result<Value, Value>, so an interruption inside a native (a callback's, a nested
evaluation's, an Atomics.wait a cancellation woke) leaves it as its result or a catchable throw,
and the poll after the native is what turns it back into the interruption. Without it three tests
fail: host_interruption_wakes_a_blocked_atomics_wait, interruption_stops_an_endless_microtask_
chain and a_handle_swap_moves_shadow_realm_interpreters_too ("realm.evaluate('for (;;) {}') threw
: undefined"). Its cost when nothing is armed: an atomic load and a branch
(RuntimeInterrupt::current_reason reads the state word; a deadline armed adds the clock). Natives
carrying the interruption in their error type, the exemplars' way, is left for later as a
refactor of NativeFn.

X86-64. A known difference: x86-64's generic call helper's cached calls (Interp::call_jit_cached
-> call_native_entry, which Rust callers share) keep the whole boundary; extending B2 there needs
a variant of call_jit_cached for generated code only. x86-64 is the secondary platform and is not
measured; the two B2 poll tests are ARM64's.

perf's instruction count gives (the sampler drops what arrives while it records), so the column

What V8 does for the same steps (builtins-regexp-gen.cc; regexp.tq): the fast path's test is one
map compare and a positive-Smi lastIndex (IsFastRegExpNoPrototype, :1166-1191), lastIndex a field
load (:149-155); RegExpExecInternal (:752-1100) checks lastIndex against the length, unpacks the
string (ToDirect), dispatches on the data's type tag, runs two quick reject filters (a mask over
four characters and a start-character bitset, :826-889), loads the code for the encoding and calls
it with nine arguments (:982-1040), about 70-90 instructions around the irregexp code. JSC's
execInline (runtime/RegExpObjectInlines.h:214-250) reads lastIndex as a UInt32 (:188-206) and calls
RegExp::matchInline with the RegExp's own ovector.

What TRust does that they do not, found so far:
- slot_last_index's main path is about 50 instructions of 141 (the env flag's OnceLock, the
  protector's RefCell, the object's borrow, the slot's cell-or-record branch, the NaN-box decode).
- note_execution stores a tier tick and the subject's storage on every exec, even once the width's
  code exists; V8 ticks only while the bytecode runs (src/regexp/regexp.cc:842-862).
- The diagnostics gates (the census, the profile, the native verifier) are separate OnceLock
  acquire loads, three to five an exec.

Cuts so far (worktree c3-wt4, branch p2-c3-entry, on d029ec80):
- E1 d54945b6: alloc_shape reads RegExpAlloc's shape from an Interp copy, one compare.
- E2 6f79a17a: the tier ticks and the storage feedback stop once a width is decided.
- E1 recommitted as b6b62fd1 (the same code as d54945b6, with the tests the coordinator asked
  for: regexps_of_every_realm_share_the_shape_execs_lastindex_read_compares and
  exec_reads_lastindex_at_its_slot_only_when_it_is_a_plain_number) and E2 as bf4003c8. The Interp's
  copy of RegExpAlloc's shape does not travel with Realm switches: a shape records keys and
  attributes in the Agent's transition table and the [[Prototype]] is the object's own field, so
  every Realm's RegExps share it (the protector keeps instance_shape across invalidation for the
  same reason).

### TRust: the engine's incremental marking steps in the page actor's and workers' idle time (record, 2026-11-07)

Landed in TRust's main by fast-forward, 78435d0 to 8bd6b3f (local, unpushed; the coordinator's, as
the engine handoff's port; an agent's change). TRust needs no other port for P2's final engine: its
builds on 30b266ee, whose crates tree main 447af048 has, compile and pass as below. The agent's record:

1. THE CHANGE
TRust 8bd6b3f, branch p2-idle-marking (from TRust main 78435d0; worktree target/p2/djot-gap/trust-idle),
src/trust_js_backend.rs +33. advance_idle_marking() takes one Engine::advance_incremental_marking step
(a slice of at most a millisecond, or the cycle's final pause) where the actor would otherwise wait:
in the page actor's idle path beside the memory reducer (inside `if !defer_task_gc`, so never during an
input burst) and in each worker's loop. While a cycle still runs, `wait` becomes zero and the timeout a
maintenance wake (Wake::Maintenance, WorkerTask::Checkpoint): the loop takes whatever work arrived, and
then the next step. The engine's step itself refuses inside JS execution or GC suppression.

2. GROUNDING (V8 c8b709085e, files in target/p2/w6/src/v8)
- The incremental marking job's runner is the foreground task runner at TaskPriority::kUserVisible
  (src/heap/incremental-marking-job.cc:46-51).
- ScheduleTask posts the task, non-nestable when the platform allows, without delay
  (incremental-marking-job.cc:53-78; PostNonNestableTask 67, PostTask 69).
- Task::RunInternal calls AdvanceAndFinalizeIfComplete (128) and posts the next task while major
  marking continues (134) (incremental-marking-job.cc:80-137).
- A task's step is 1 ms (kMaxStepSizeOnTask, src/heap/incremental-marking.cc:56).
- Each worker isolate has its own heap and so its own job.

3. THE DIFFERENCE FROM V8
V8's step is a user-visible-priority task that interleaves with the other tasks. TRust's step runs only
when the actor's queues are empty, and not during an input burst (defer_task_gc, as the memory
reducer). A page that never idles behaves as before the change: allocation-driven slices and the
cycle's final pause advance its cycles.

4. WHAT THE REPLAY HARNESS AND THE SPIKE MEASURE: A PAGE THAT NEVER IDLES (idle-checks.txt)
Neither runs the resident actor. trust-browser-replay calls trust::js::transform, a one-shot document
run that advances its task sources back to back in virtual time until they are quiescent;
trust-js-spike calls run_benchmark, a one-shot loop that dispatches each timer at once
(nextDeadline). Neither ever waits, so the step never runs: they show a page that never idles.
TRust 8bd6b3f against 78435d0, release on engine bf4003c8 and debug-assertions on 77d2c414 (the same
engine code), as trust-checks.sh runs them:
- The three pages complete, valid and with main-off's output on both sides, in release, dbg-1 and
  dbg-force (TRUST_JS_GC_VERIFY=1 under TRUST_JS_GC_INCREMENTAL=1 and =force).
- Their slices are the same on both sides: release dom-reconcile 130 (all allocation), Vue 112 (63
  allocation, 49 the engine's own task-boundary collections), event-loop 0; dbg-1 60 each; dbg-force
  17639-17657 (allocation).
- The spike passes on both sides: release scores 3576 and 3566 (single unheld runs), 8 cycle majors
  each; dbg-1 988 and 1424, dbg-force 703 and 901 (loaded machine). Every slice is allocation-driven
  but 1-3 of the engine's task-boundary ones.

5. THE IDLE STEP IN THE RESIDENT ACTOR: TRUST-HEADLESS (headless-checks.txt, headless/)
trust-headless drives the shared BrowserController and so the resident page actor, in real time.
Binaries on engine 30b266ee (E1/E2 on the hardening series e49d4433 on candidate 2 dad9d67f, the
expected final tree): fidle = TRust 8bd6b3f, fbase = 78435d0. Pages from site/: the three replay
pages (Vue's js and css beside them) with --settle 12, so the actor sits idle past the memory
reducer's 8 s; the spike's run.js as a page (spike.html), which in a window yields between its steps
with setTimeout(RunStep, 25) (run.js:148), each timer's lateness recorded; and latency.html, a kept
400,000-object list and then a 25 ms timer chain of 640 ticks (16 s), each tick's lateness recorded.
The accounting (gc-cycles.py) classes a slice or final pause as allocation, the engine's task
boundary ([gc-task] follows), the reducer's start (a TaskBoundary start), or an idle step (the other
TaskBoundary slices); a final pause after an idle step that completed the marking is idle-done (the
actor loop's next small allocation takes it while the actor is idle).
- Every page's text is the same on both sides in release, dbg-1 and dbg-force: dom-reconcile
  aea5c013e75c, Vue 75c5617cff93, event-loop 60feabeb3468. No JS errors and no panics, with heap
  verification on in the dbg runs.
- Vue, release. fidle: 3 cycles, the memory reducer's two finished idle: 141 steps, 19.8 ms, the
  longest 0.88 ms; their final pauses 14.5 ms, the longest 11.3 ms; per cycle 11.5 ms of marking in
  idle time against 6.4 ms in script time; the heap ends at 6.10 MB, 19,410 objects. fbase: the
  reducer's cycle starts (one 3.3 ms slice) and stays open until exit, and the heap stays at
  11.9 MB, 39,320 objects. dbg-1 the same on Vue and event-loop (2 of 3 cycles finished idle on
  fidle; a cycle open at exit on fbase). dbg-force: fidle's idle steps run between the forced
  allocation slices (Vue 378, event-loop 544), fbase has none.
- Without the step a reducer-started cycle never finishes while the page is idle. Before e49d4433
  the reducer took a running cycle as its own (gc_start_cycle_for_host returned true while one ran)
  and did not advance it either, so fbase's open cycle predates that change; with e49d4433 the
  reducer also starts no other while it is open. The step is the embedder's half of V8's
  IncrementalMarkingJob, which every V8 embedder runs through its task runner.
- dom-reconcile: one allocation-driven cycle on both sides; no step runs.
- The spike page, release: no step runs on either side. Its cycles start and finish inside run.js's
  long steps, so no cycle runs in a 25 ms gap.
- The latency page, release (unheld): fidle 1,384 idle steps between the ticks, the longest
  1.88 ms; the reducer's two cycles finished idle; lateness mean 1.24 ms, p99 2.00, max 2.60. fbase
  no steps, a cycle open at exit; lateness mean 1.36, p99 2.60, max 3.30.
- The latency page under debug assertions: dbg-1 fidle 195 steps (5.4 s: verification after every
  slice of a 40 MB heap makes a step up to 73 ms), 2 cycles finished idle, fbase a cycle open at
  exit; both finish with no JS errors or panics. dbg-force: each tick outlasts its 25 ms (forced
